# Dry Water

The room smelled like mildew and cold concrete. Marcus lay on the plywood table at a slight incline, his wrists chafing against the zip ties that anchored him to a steel ring bolted to the wood beneath him. His ankles were strapped. His chest was pinned. Above him, a fluorescent tube hummed and flickered, casting everything in that sick hospital pallor.

He had been here—how long? Hours. Maybe a day. Time had come unmoored.

The towel came first. He saw it in the hands of the man in the gray uniform—the same man who had been methodically laying out supplies on a metal tray beside the table. The towel was dark, thick, terrycloth. It was wet before it reached his face.

It covered him from hairline to chin. The world went black and warm and wet.

*What are my orders? Where is the convoy route?*

The questions were calm. Conversational. Almost bored.

Marcus tried to keep his jaw set, his breathing slow. *Don't give them anything. Don't give them anything.*

Then the water came.

It didn't pour—it *poured*, like someone had cracked open the ceiling and released the sky. It hit the towel and the towel became a mask and the mask became a seal, and suddenly the water had nowhere to go except *in*. Into his nose. Into his mouth. Into the back of his throat, where it pooled and spread and choked.

His body lurched against the restraints before he told it to.

Every instinct he had ever possessed, every animal claw buried beneath ten thousand years of civilization, *screamed*. His legs thrashed against the plywood. His fingers curled and uncurled, grasping for anything—anything at all—to push the water away, to rip the towel from his face, to claw free air that existed just inches beyond the cloth.

He couldn't breathe.

That was the thing they never told you in training. You imagined it would be like being held underwater at the pool, a pressure, a pushing. But it wasn't like that at all. It was like being buried alive with water. It was like a sink had been driven into his skull and someone had turned the handle to its fullest, and the water was *filling* him, pressing into every cavity in his sinuses and his throat and his lungs, and it *would not stop*, and the air that should have been there simply *wasn't*.

His chest convulsed. His diaphragm spasmed, trying to draw a breath that wasn't there. Every muscle in his torso clenched in a single, rolling cramp that bent him against the table like a bridge. The zip ties cut into his wrists. He could hear himself making a sound—low, guttural, half voice and half animal—but it was muffled beneath the water and the towel and the ringing that was starting in his ears.

*What are the supply routes?*

He would tell them. He was already telling them, or trying to—some part of his brain was firing the words, *not it, not that, I don't know, please*—but the words dissolved into the water. It didn't matter. The panic had overtaken the language center entirely. There was no longer a strategic mind making calculated decisions about what to withhold. There was only the reptile brain, the amygdala, the thing that lived at the base of the skull and had one message and one message only:

*I am drowning. I am drowning. I am drowning.*

And the cruelest part—the part he would think about for years afterward, in the dark, in the cold sweat of 3 a.m.—was that he *knew* he wasn't drowning. His rational mind was still there, pressed flat and screaming beneath the animal terror, and it was saying: *You are on a table. You are on dry land. You are in a concrete room in a country whose name you know. They will not let you die. This is not water. This is not the sea.*

But the body didn't care. The body had passed through the membrane between thought and reflex and arrived at a place where the only language was the thrashing of limbs and the arching of a spine and the convulsive, machine-gun rhythm of a diaphragm trying to breathe through sealed sinuses and a mouth full of water that would not stop.

It was worse than the fear of death. It was the fear of death performed on a loop, over and over, with no conclusion. Death at least was an end. This was a door that kept opening and closing and opening and closing.

The water stopped.

It stopped as suddenly as it had started, and the towel was pulled away, and air—blessed, stupid, miracle air—rushed into his face and his chest expanded and he *gasped*, a single enormous hitching breath that came with a sound so loud and so ragged that it didn't seem human. Water ran from his nose and his mouth and his ears. His eyes were squeezed shut against the fluorescent light. He tasted chlorine and salt and something metallic that was the inside of his own bloodied nose.

He coughed—a full body event, his torso folding in half against the restraints—and water erupted from him in a thin, violent spray.

He breathed. Once. Twice. Three times.

The air tasted like everything he had ever loved.

His chest heaved. His fingers trembled so badly that his hands looked like they were being electrocuted. A sound was still coming from him—half sob, half breath—and he couldn't stop it any more than he could stop his heart from hammering.

*Where is the supply route?*

Marcus opened his mouth. The words were *right there*. The intel, the coordinates, the names—they were climbing over each other in his throat like rats in a barrel, desperate to spill out into the light. Every cell of him wanted to surrender. Not out of cowardice. Not out of betrayal. But because the drowning thing in his brain stem was saying: *Tell them and it stops. Tell them and it stops. Tell them and it—*

"…I…" His voice was a ruin. He swallowed. Tried again. "I don't…"

*Are you ready to cooperate?*

His lips moved. The words were there. Three names. Four numbers. A road.

The man in gray leaned in, patient as a priest.

Marcus closed his eyes.

The towel came back.

The water stopped.

It stopped as suddenly as it had started, and the towel was pulled away, and air—blessed, stupid, miracle air—rushed into his face and his chest expanded and he gasped, a single enormous hitching breath that came with a sound so loud and so ragged that it didn't seem human. Water ran from his nose and his mouth and his ears. His eyes were squeezed shut against the fluorescent light. He tasted chlorine and salt and something metallic that was the inside of his own bloodied nose.

He coughed—a full body event, his torso folding in half against the restraints—and water erupted from him in a thin, violent spray.

He breathed. Once. Twice. Three times.

The air tasted like everything he had ever loved.

His chest heaved. His fingers trembled so badly that his hands looked like they were being electrocuted. A sound was still coming from him—half sob, half breath—and he couldn't stop it any more than he could stop his heart from hammering.

His lips moved. The words were there. Three names. Four numbers. A road.

The man in gray leaned in, patient as a priest.

Marcus closed his eyes.

The towel came back.

The snow had swallowed every sound except his own ragged breathing and the drumbeat of paws behind him. Then even that breathing stopped as his back hit the boulder — a cold, unyielding slab of gray stone slick with ice — and there was nowhere left to run.

They circled. Eight, maybe nine shapes that were more darkness than body, their eyes catching what little light the bone-white world still offered. The lead wolf stood apart, broad-shouldered, its breath pluming in slow, patient clouds. It studied him the way the cold studied all living things — with quiet certainty.

Then it moved.

There was no warning snarl, no dramatic lunge through the air like some storybook beast. The wolf simply stepped forward and *bit* — a precise, devastating clamp of its jaws into the meat of his upper arm, just above the elbow. The sound was nothing. A soft, wet compression, like a boot pressing into deep mud. And for one impossible half-second, it didn't hurt at all.

The cold had been his whole world for hours. It had settled into his bones like a second skeleton, made his fingers into useless clubs, turned his skin into something that felt like hide. He had *forgotten* what warmth was.

Then the pain arrived — and with it, heat.

It rushed up his arm like a lit fuse. Not the gentle warmth of a fire or a blanket but something violent and cellular, a furious announcement from his own body: *you are breaking.* The wolf's teeth were a ring of white fire around his arm, each fang a distinct point of agony driving deeper, deeper into tissue he didn't know he possessed.

And then the blood came.

It spilled over the wolf's muzzle and instantly steamed against the snow — a thin, pink mist rising where drops hit the drift and vanished, one temperature annihilating another. The heat of it was staggering. Blood had never felt like this before — like he was holding his own heart in the open air. It ran down his forearm in a slick, tacky river, hot enough to briefly thaw the frost on his skin before the arctic wind stole it away and turned his wrist to ice again. Hot and cold and hot and cold, an agonizing negotiation between his body and the world.

He could *feel* the snowflakes landing on his lips — tiny, clean, cold crystals — while warmth pulsed and dripped from the wound inches away. The wolf shook its head once, side to side, and the arm came alive with a wet, grinding radiance. His vision whitened. The cold of the snow beneath his knees felt like it belonged to another man, someone numb and distant and safe. The heat of his blood felt like the only real thing left in the universe.

The other wolves were moving in now, their footsteps muffled and soft. But he barely felt them against the howling conversation happening in his arm — the wolf's furnacelike grip clamped shut against his blood's desperate, singing escape. Two temperatures fighting in one small place.

The snow kept falling. It landed on the open wound with pinpricks of cold so sharp they were almost bright, almost tasteable, each flake a tiny blue star against the furnace of exposed flesh.

He had never known the body could contain so much temperature at once.

# Neon Warrant

## Part I: The Mark

The rain in Neo-Shanghai never washed anything clean. It only smeared the neon further—colors bleeding across the perpetual wet, painting the lower streets in fever-dream hues of magenta and electric blue.

Kael Voss moved through the crowd like a ghost in a steel-gray trenchcoat, its adaptive camouflage fabric flickering faintly as it tried to match the chaotic wallpaper of the market district. His left eye—the one that still worked without assistance—scanned faces in the crowd. His right eye was a Vantage-7 ocular implant, capable of running facial recognition, thermal imaging, and threat assessment simultaneously. It painted the world in overlapping layers of data only he could see.

A translucent dossier hovered in the corner of his vision.

**TARGET: ELENA CHO**
**WANTED FOR: Corporate espionage, murder of three Helios Dynamics security personnel, possession of stolen neural-interface prototypes**
**BOUNTY: 420,000 credits**
**THREAT ASSESSMENT: Moderate to High. Target is cybernetically augmented. Likely armed. Known tactical background — former corporate intelligence operative.**

Kael dismissed the dossier with a blink.

He didn't need to be reminded twice. He'd spent three weeks tracking Elena Cho across three city-states and two orbital stations. She was smart—brilliant, actually. The kind of smart that got people killed, including herself, eventually. She'd stolen something the wrong people needed back, and she'd killed to get it. Now the wrong people wanted their prize returned and their pound of flesh paid, and Kael was the instrument of that transaction.

He found her not because he was cleverer than she was. He found her because of one fatal mistake: a moment of sentiment. She'd sent an encrypted message to a contact in the old quarter—a mother, a childhood friend, someone who still mattered to her after everything. Kael had intercepted the signal transmission patterns with a black-market signal interceptor bought on the Rust Deck, and they'd pointed him here. To this rain-soaked market. To the noodle stall at the end of Corridor 12.

He spotted her sitting alone at a battered metal table under the awning of a food vendor, a bowl of something steaming in front of her. She looked different from her dossier photo—thinner, shorter hair, a faint scar tracing her left jawline—but the thermal signature matching the implant in her left hand gave her away. It ran hotter than natural tissue. A wireless data-jack, illegally modded. The kind you could use to interface with systems you weren't supposed to touch.

She was eating slowly. Deliberately. The way someone eats when they know they might not get another meal.

*Don't make it personal*, Kael reminded himself. But he'd been doing this for eleven years, and it never got easier to watch people eat.

He stopped at a stall ten meters away, pretending to examine the wares—cheap neural-interface dongles and bootleg holographic fans. His right eye locked onto her and began tracking. His hand moved slowly to the holster under his coat.

## Part II: The Moment

He chose his approach carefully. Direct confrontation, hands visible, peaceable expression. Even a cornered rat runs if it feels the trap too early. He'd close to three meters, present himself, and offer her the choice: surrender quietly, or don't. He always gave them the choice.

He stepped out from behind the stall and walked toward her.

Elena Cho saw him coming at four meters. He saw the exact moment recognition hit—her pupils dilated, her jaw tightened, and her right hand dropped beneath the table where she'd concealed a weapon.

"Don't," Kael said. His voice was flat. Calm. Not unkind, but not warm. A surgeon's voice before the first incision. "I have a warrant. It's valid. You know how this works."

Elena stared at him. Her eyes were dark and intelligent and very, very afraid behind the defiance.

"You're Voss," she said. "I've heard the name."

"Then you know I don't miss."

"I've heard that too." Her hand stayed under the table. "But you should know—I didn't kill those guards for fun. What I took from Helios, I took because it needed to be taken. The neural-interface prototypes they were developing—Voss, they weren't designing tools. They were designing *leashes*. Controlled-compliance hardware. They were going to wire it into their workforce's new implant packages. Every worker would be pacified. Controlled. *Owned*."

"That's a story for a jury."

"There won't be a jury. There will be a boardroom and a quiet disposal." Her voice cracked slightly. She pulled it back. "You know I'm right."

Kael knew she might be right. He'd read the case files on the way over—redacted, but he knew how to read between the blackout bars. Helios Dynamics had a reputation that smelled like ozone and ethics violations. But a warrant was a warrant, and the credits were real, and the world didn't wait for moral clarity.

"I understand," he said, and he meant it. "Come with me. I'll make sure you get a fair hearing. I have contacts—"

"You have a *price*."

He didn't deny it. "Right now, the best I can offer is that I don't hurt you."

For a long moment, the rain filled the silence. Water drummed on the corrugated awning overhead. Somewhere far above, a transport drone hummed past the towers.

Then Elena moved.

It was fast—militarily fast. She surged to her feet and kicked the table toward him, scattering the bowl and its contents. Her right hand came up from beneath the table holding a compact kinetic pistol—illegal as hell, projectile-based in an era of energy weapons, but projectile weapons were still lethal, and she knew what she was doing. The pistol spat twice.

Kael was already moving. He'd anticipated this—had been anticipating it since the first step toward her. His trenchcoat's reactive armor plate hardened along his torso as he threw himself to the left. The first shot struck his right shoulder and the armor absorbed it with a brutal jolt that sent his arm numb. The second shot tore through the awning above and sent a gout of sparks raining down from a severed light conduit.

The market dissolved into chaos. Shoppers screamed and scattered. Stall keepers ducked behind their counters. A vendor's cart toppled, sending cheap electronics skittering across the wet ground.

Elena was already running. She vaulted over a low barrier and cut left into a narrow maintenance corridor between buildings—the kind of alley that didn't show up on tourist maps. Kael pushed off the wet ground and gave chase.

His shoulder screamed at him. The armor had done its job, but the impact had bruised bone and torn muscle beneath. Pain was a tool—it sharpened focus if you didn't let it sharpen panic. He ran through it.

The corridor was dark, lit only by the red glow of emergency light strips along the floor. Steam hissed from pipes overhead. Elena was thirty meters ahead and moving fast, her augmented legs carrying her with an unnatural grace.

"Stop running!" he shouted. His voice echoed off the narrow walls.

She didn't stop. She slammed through a door at the corridor's end and burst into a wider passage—a service level beneath the market, filled with utility vehicles and stacked cargo containers. She scrambled up a stack of shipping crates and was running along the tops of them, gaining height and vantage.

Kael drew his weapon.

It was called a *Voltaic Constriction Sidearm*, VCS-9, manufactured by Cobalt Tactical Systems. A stun weapon, specifically engineered for bounty enforcement. It looked like a bulky, angular pistol with two electrode prongs extending from the muzzle and a capacitive cylinder running along the underbarrel that hummed faintly with stored charge. It fired a concentrated electrical arc at a target up to fifteen meters away, delivering a precisely modulated high-voltage, low-amperence pulse designed to incapacitate a human being without—ideally—killing them.

Kael raised it and tracked Elena as she leapt from crate to crate.

Last warning. He always gave the last warning.

"Freeze, Elena! This is your last chance!"

She looked back at him. She was panting, wild-eyed, cornered in her own way. She raised her kinetic pistol again.

*She's going to shoot me.*

This time, she aimed for the head.

Kael didn't wait.

## Part III: The Shot

The VCS-9 emitted a sharp, crackling discharge—a sound like a whip-crack crossed with tearing fabric—and a visible arc of white-blue electricity leapt from the electrode prongs in a directed beam. The air itself ionized along its path, leaving a faint ozone stink and a ghostly afterimage that hung in the damp air for a fraction of a second.

The arc struck Elena Cho square in the center of her torso.

The effect was immediate, violent, and total.

**The Electrical Shock and the Human Body**

The human body is, at its most fundamental level, an electrochemical machine. Every thought, every muscle contraction, every heartbeat is governed by tiny electrical signals—ionic gradients across cell membranes, neurotransmitters released in response to voltage shifts. The brain is a battery. The nerves are wires. The muscles are electrochemical engines. When an external electrical force overrides this delicate internal system, the results are catastrophic and precisely measurable.

The VCS-9 delivered a high-voltage pulse—approximately 50,000 volts at peak—into Elena's body at the point of contact. Voltage is the *pressure* of electricity, the force that drives current. High voltage is necessary to overcome the electrical resistance of human skin and the air gap between the weapon and its target. But it is the *amperage*—the actual flow of electrical current—that does the damage. The VCS-9 was engineered to deliver current in a carefully controlled burst: enough to overwhelm the nervous system, but limited in duration and total charge to reduce the risk of fatality.

The current entered Elena's body through the skin of her chest at the point where the arc struck. Even though the weapon was designed with safeguards, the initial contact was brutal.

**First Effects — Instantaneous Neuromuscular Override:**

The electrical current raced through her body along the paths of least resistance—which, in the human body, are the nerves, blood vessels, and muscle tissue. Electricity does not pass through bone with the same ease, but soft tissue is highly conductive, especially when damp with sweat or, in this case, rain.

As the current passed through her skeletal muscles, it caused **tetanic contraction**—a state in which every muscle fiber in the current's path is forced to contract simultaneously and cannot release. The body's own electrical signals, which carefully choreograph which muscles contract and when, were completely drowned out by the external charge. The result is the characteristic "locking up" seen in electrocution: limbs rigid, back arched, hands clamped shut.

Elena's body seized. Her arms flew rigid to her sides, fingers splayed then clenched into impossible fists. Her legs locked completely, and for one terrible frozen instant, she stood atop the cargo crates like a statue—arms out, back bowed, mouth open in a scream that her diaphragm and intercostal muscles couldn't produce because they, too, were locked in forced contraction.

Her kinetic pistol fell from her hand and clattered down the side of the crates.

**Cardiac Disruption:**

Some of the current passed through her thoracic cavity and through the heart. The heart is an electrochemical pump in the most literal sense—a specialized muscle controlled by the sinoatrial node, which generates rhythmic electrical impulses that cause coordinated contraction of the atria and ventricles. The external current disrupted this rhythm.

This is the most dangerous effect of any electrical shock on the body: **cardiac arrhythmia**. The ventricular muscle fibers, receiving an external electrical stimulus, contracted in chaotic, uncoordinated fashion rather than the orderly wave that pumps blood. For a brief, terrifying moment, Elena's heart entered a state of **ventricular fibrillation**—quivering rather than beating, pumping no meaningful blood to her brain or lungs.

**Neurological Effects:**

The current also swept through her nervous system like a forest fire through underbrush. Sensory neurons fired wildly, sending massive, overwhelming signals to her brain—pain, pressure, heat, and a hundred contradictory sensations all at once. Motor neurons fired indiscriminately. Even neurons in her autonomic nervous system, which regulate involuntary functions, were disrupted.

This caused immediate **autonomic dysfunction**. Her pupils dilated abruptly. Saliva production surged or ceased, depending on which nerves were most affected. Her bladder and bowel sphincters lost tone. Her blood pressure spiked as adrenal glands dumped adrenaline and cortisol into her bloodstream in response to the electrical trauma—a survival response with no practical application in this moment, since her body couldn't do anything with the flood of stress hormones.

**Respiratory System:**

Elena's diaphragm and intercostal muscles—the muscles of breathing—were locked in tetanic contraction, just like every other skeletal muscle in the current's path. She could not inhale. She could not exhale. Her lungs held their last breath like a sealed vault. Oxygen in her blood began to drop immediately.

**Pain:**

If there is a single word to describe the sensation of a high-voltage electrical shock passing through the human body, it is **totality**. There is no specific location of pain because the pain is *everywhere* simultaneously. The overwhelming stimulation of every pain receptor along the current's path creates a sensation beyond ordinary experience—not just hurt, but a kind of existential violation. The body's most basic systems are being hijacked. Every alarm in the nervous system is ringing at maximum volume with no volume knob to turn down.

Many survivors of electrical shock report that the pain is not remembered as pain in the usual sense. They describe it as a "white light," a "roar," a "seizure of being." The body does not have a frame of reference for this degree of neuromuscular overwhelm. It is, in a very real sense, the sensation of your own bioelectricity being replaced by something foreign and violent.

---

**The Pulse Ended.**

The VCS-9 was designed to deliver its charge in a controlled burst of approximately 2.5 seconds. A prolonged delivery risked ventricular fibrillation that wouldn't spontaneously resolve, burns at the electrode entry and exit points, and thermal damage to internal tissues. Two and a half seconds was enough.

The white-blue arc died. The crackling silence that followed was somehow louder than the discharge itself.

Elena Cho's body—released from tetanic contraction—went completely limp. Every muscle, exhausted by the involuntary maximal contractions, simply *let go*. She crumpled backward off the cargo crates and fell three meters to the concrete floor below.

She hit hard. But Kael had been watching the readout on his wrist-mounted diagnostics—patched into the VCS-9's telemetry—and he'd seen her heart rhythm begin to recover from fibrillation within a second of the pulse ending. The body's natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, had reasserted control. She was in pain. She was disoriented. She was alive.

He crossed the space quickly, holstering the VCS-9 and pulling from his belt a pair of **Neural Bind Cuffs**—the standard restraint system for augmented targets. They clamped around Elena's wrists and immediately interfaced with her cybernetic implants, sending a low-level inhibitory signal that prevented any augmented reflexes or combat systems from activating.

Elena lay on the wet concrete, shaking. Not the full-body convulsion of the shock itself, but the aftershocks—small, violent tremors that rippled through her muscles as they tried to recalibrate after being overwhelmed. Her chest was heaving now, each breath a raw, ragged gasp as her respiratory muscles resumed function. Tears streamed from her eyes—partly from pain, partly from the involuntary irritation of the lacrimal glands during the shock, partly from grief.

Her chest, where the arc had struck, showed a **small, shallow burn mark**—a branching, fern-like pattern called a **Lichtenberg figure**, where the current entered the skin. The skin there was reddened and blistered at the center. Around it, the superficial capillaries in the skin had ruptured from the current's heat, leaving faint red lines that looked almost decorative, like a scar in the shape of a frozen lightning bolt.

Her muscles continued to spasm intermittently—twitches in her legs, a jerk in her left arm, a flutter in her jaw that made her teeth chatter involuntarily. These were the lingering neurological aftereffects. The motor neurons, still firing in the aftermath of the external stimulus, needed time to settle.

Kael knelt beside her. He checked her pulse—rapid, thready, but present. Her pupils were reactive. She was conscious.

"Elena," he said. "You're alive. Stay still. Don't try to move."

She looked up at him with eyes that held no rage now—only a vast, hollow exhaustion.

"The prototypes," she whispered. Her voice was shredded, raw from the scream she couldn't produce. "They're in my apartment. Sub-level 4, Building 97. I tagged the case with a dead-man's code. If I don't deactivate it in... fourteen hours... the data deletes itself."

"I'll make sure it gets recovered."

"And the story? Will anyone hear the story?"

Kael hesitated. The rain dripped through the broken ceiling of the service level, spattering on the concrete around them.

"I don't know," he said. And then, quietly: "But I'll tell it."

## Part IV: Extraction

He pulled her to her feet—gently, one arm under her shoulders. She could barely stand. Her legs were rubbery and uncoordinated, muscles still misfiring from the neuromuscular trauma. He half-carried her to the service level exit, where his vehicle—a matte-black tactical skimmer—waited with its engine purring.

He eased her into the passenger seat and wrapped her in a thermal blanket. Her body temperature had dropped noticeably during the shock—electrical current can disrupt thermoregulation—and the trembling hadn't stopped.

As he guided the skimmer up through the rain toward the upper levels and the detention facility on Ward 7, Kael Voss looked at the woman shivering in his passenger seat. Forty-two thousand credits. That's what he'd been paid to bring her in. Enough to clear his debts and fund the next contract.

He thought about neural-interface prototypes and controlled-compliance hardware and a world where people's own implants could be used to make them obey.

He thought about how she'd stopped to eat a bowl of noodles before the end.

The rain kept falling. It smeared the neon further.

It never washed anything clean.

---

*END*

He chose his approach carefully. Direct confrontation, hands visible, peaceable expression. Even a cornered rat runs if it feels the trap too early. He'd close to three meters, present himself, and offer her the choice: surrender quietly, or don't. He always gave them the choice.

He stepped out from behind the stall and walked toward her.

Elena Cho saw him coming at four meters. He saw the exact moment recognition hit—her pupils dilated, her jaw tightened, and her right hand dropped beneath the table where she'd concealed a weapon.

"Don't," Kael said. His voice was flat. Calm. Not unkind, but not warm. A surgeon's voice before the first incision. "I have a warrant. It's valid. You know how this works."

Elena stared at him. Her eyes were dark and intelligent and very, very afraid behind the defiance.

"You're Voss," she said. "I've heard the name."

"Then you know I don't miss."

"I've heard that too." Her hand stayed under the table. "But you should know—I didn't kill those guards for fun. What I took from Helios, I took because it needed to be taken. The neural-interface prototypes they were developing—Voss, they weren't designing tools. They were designing leashes. Controlled-compliance hardware. They were going to wire it into their workforce's new implant packages. Every worker would be pacified. Controlled. Owned."

"That's a story for a jury."

"There won't be a jury. There will be a boardroom and a quiet disposal." Her voice cracked slightly. She pulled it back. "You know I'm right."

Kael knew she might be right. He'd read the case files on the way over—redacted, but he knew how to read between the blackout bars. Helios Dynamics had a reputation that smelled like ozone and ethics violations. But a warrant was a warrant, and the credits were real, and the world didn't wait for moral clarity.

"I understand," he said, and he meant it. "Come with me. I'll make sure you get a fair hearing. I have contacts—"

"You have a price."

He didn't deny it. "Right now, the best I can offer is that I don't hurt you."

For a long moment, the rain filled the silence. Water drummed on the corrugated awning overhead. Somewhere far above, a transport drone hummed past the towers.

Then Elena moved.

It was fast—militarily fast. She surged to her feet and kicked the table toward him, scattering the bowl and its contents. Her right hand came up from beneath the table holding a compact kinetic pistol—illegal as hell, projectile-based in an era of energy weapons, but projectile weapons were still lethal, and she knew what she was doing. The pistol spat twice.

Kael was already moving. He'd anticipated this—had been anticipating it since the first step toward her. His trenchcoat's reactive armor plate hardened along his torso as he threw himself to the left. The first shot struck his right shoulder and the armor absorbed it with a brutal jolt that sent his arm numb. The second shot tore through the awning above and sent a gout of sparks raining down from a severed light conduit.

The market dissolved into chaos. Shoppers screamed and scattered. Stall keepers ducked behind their counters. A vendor's cart toppled, sending cheap electronics skittering across the wet ground.

Elena was already running. She vaulted over a low barrier and cut left into a narrow maintenance corridor between buildings—the kind of alley that didn't show up on tourist maps. Kael pushed off the wet ground and gave chase.

His shoulder screamed at him. The armor had done its job, but the impact had bruised bone and torn muscle beneath. Pain was a tool—it sharpened focus if you didn't let it sharpen panic. He ran through it.

The corridor was dark, lit only by the red glow of emergency light strips along the floor. Steam hissed from pipes overhead. Elena was thirty meters ahead and moving fast, her augmented legs carrying her with an unnatural grace.

"Stop running!" he shouted. His voice echoed off the narrow walls.

She didn't stop. She slammed through a door at the corridor's end and burst into a wider passage—a service level beneath the market, filled with utility vehicles and stacked cargo containers. She scrambled up a stack of shipping crates and was running along the tops of them, gaining height and vantage.

Kael drew his weapon.

It was called a Voltaic Constriction Sidearm, VCS-9, manufactured by Cobalt Tactical Systems. A stun weapon, specifically engineered for bounty enforcement. It looked like a bulky, angular pistol with two electrode prongs extending from the muzzle and a capacitive cylinder running along the underbarrel that hummed faintly with stored charge. It fired a concentrated electrical arc at a target up to fifteen meters away, delivering a precisely modulated high-voltage, low-amperence pulse designed to incapacitate a human being without—ideally—killing them.

Kael raised it and tracked Elena as she leapt from crate to crate.

Last warning. He always gave the last warning.

"Freeze, Elena! This is your last chance!"

She looked back at him. She was panting, wild-eyed, cornered in her own way. She raised her kinetic pistol again.

She's going to shoot me.

This time, she aimed for the head.

Kael didn't wait.

Part III: The Shot

The VCS-9 emitted a sharp, crackling discharge—a sound like a whip-crack crossed with tearing fabric—and a visible arc of white-blue electricity leapt from the electrode prongs in a directed beam. The air itself ionized along its path, leaving a faint ozone stink and a ghostly afterimage that hung in the damp air for a fraction of a second.

The arc struck Elena Cho square in the center of her torso.

The effect was immediate, violent, and total.

The Electrical Shock and the Human Body

The human body is, at its most fundamental level, an electrochemical machine. Every thought, every muscle contraction, every heartbeat is governed by tiny electrical signals—ionic gradients across cell membranes, neurotransmitters released in response to voltage shifts. The brain is a battery. The nerves are wires. The muscles are electrochemical engines. When an external electrical force overrides this delicate internal system, the results are catastrophic and precisely measurable.

The VCS-9 delivered a high-voltage pulse—approximately 50,000 volts at peak—into Elena's body at the point of contact. Voltage is the pressure of electricity, the force that drives current. High voltage is necessary to overcome the electrical resistance of human skin and the air gap between the weapon and its target. But it is the amperage—the actual flow of electrical current—that does the damage. The VCS-9 was engineered to deliver current in a carefully controlled burst: enough to overwhelm the nervous system, but limited in duration and total charge to reduce the risk of fatality.

The current entered Elena's body through the skin of her chest at the point where the arc struck. Even though the weapon was designed with safeguards, the initial contact was brutal.

First Effects — Instantaneous Neuromuscular Override:

The electrical current raced through her body along the paths of least resistance—which, in the human body, are the nerves, blood vessels, and muscle tissue. Electricity does not pass through bone with the same ease, but soft tissue is highly conductive, especially when damp with sweat or, in this case, rain.

As the current passed through her skeletal muscles, it caused tetanic contraction—a state in which every muscle fiber in the current's path is forced to contract simultaneously and cannot release. The body's own electrical signals, which carefully choreograph which muscles contract and when, were completely drowned out by the external charge. The result is the characteristic "locking up" seen in electrocution: limbs rigid, back arched, hands clamped shut.

Elena's body seized. Her arms flew rigid to her sides, fingers splayed then clenched into impossible fists. Her legs locked completely, and for one terrible frozen instant, she stood atop the cargo crates like a statue—arms out, back bowed, mouth open in a scream that her diaphragm and intercostal muscles couldn't produce because they, too, were locked in forced contraction.

Her kinetic pistol fell from her hand and clattered down the side of the crates.

Cardiac Disruption:

Some of the current passed through her thoracic cavity and through the heart. The heart is an electrochemical pump in the most literal sense—a specialized muscle controlled by the sinoatrial node, which generates rhythmic electrical impulses that cause coordinated contraction of the atria and ventricles. The external current disrupted this rhythm.

This is the most dangerous effect of any electrical shock on the body: cardiac arrhythmia. The ventricular muscle fibers, receiving an external electrical stimulus, contracted in chaotic, uncoordinated fashion rather than the orderly wave that pumps blood. For a brief, terrifying moment, Elena's heart entered a state of ventricular fibrillation—quivering rather than beating, pumping no meaningful blood to her brain or lungs.

Neurological Effects:

The current also swept through her nervous system like a forest fire through underbrush. Sensory neurons fired wildly, sending massive, overwhelming signals to her brain—pain, pressure, heat, and a hundred contradictory sensations all at once. Motor neurons fired indiscriminately. Even neurons in her autonomic nervous system, which regulate involuntary functions, were disrupted.

This caused immediate autonomic dysfunction. Her pupils dilated abruptly. Saliva production surged or ceased, depending on which nerves were most affected. Her bladder and bowel sphincters lost tone. Her blood pressure spiked as adrenal glands dumped adrenaline and cortisol into her bloodstream in response to the electrical trauma—a survival response with no practical application in this moment, since her body couldn't do anything with the flood of stress hormones.

Respiratory System:

Elena's diaphragm and intercostal muscles—the muscles of breathing—were locked in tetanic contraction, just like every other skeletal muscle in the current's path. She could not inhale. She could not exhale. Her lungs held their last breath like a sealed vault. Oxygen in her blood began to drop immediately.

Pain:

If there is a single word to describe the sensation of a high-voltage electrical shock passing through the human body, it is totality. There is no specific location of pain because the pain is everywhere simultaneously. The overwhelming stimulation of every pain receptor along the current's path creates a sensation beyond ordinary experience—not just hurt, but a kind of existential violation. The body's most basic systems are being hijacked. Every alarm in the nervous system is ringing at maximum volume with no volume knob to turn down.

Many survivors of electrical shock report that the pain is not remembered as pain in the usual sense. They describe it as a "white light," a "roar," a "seizure of being." The body does not have a frame of reference for this degree of neuromuscular overwhelm. It is, in a very real sense, the sensation of your own bioelectricity being replaced by something foreign and violent.

The Pulse Ended.

The VCS-9 was designed to deliver its charge in a controlled burst of approximately 2.5 seconds. A prolonged delivery risked ventricular fibrillation that wouldn't spontaneously resolve, burns at the electrode entry and exit points, and thermal damage to internal tissues. Two and a half seconds was enough.

The white-blue arc died. The crackling silence that followed was somehow louder than the discharge itself.

Elena Cho's body—released from tetanic contraction—went completely limp. Every muscle, exhausted by the involuntary maximal contractions, simply let go. She crumpled backward off the cargo crates and fell three meters to the concrete floor below.

She hit hard. But Kael had been watching the readout on his wrist-mounted diagnostics—patched into the VCS-9's telemetry—and he'd seen her heart rhythm begin to recover from fibrillation within a second of the pulse ending. The body's natural pacemaker, the sinoatrial node, had reasserted control. She was in pain. She was disoriented. She was alive.

He crossed the space quickly, holstering the VCS-9 and pulling from his belt a pair of Neural Bind Cuffs—the standard restraint system for augmented targets. They clamped around Elena's wrists and immediately interfaced with her cybernetic implants, sending a low-level inhibitory signal that prevented any augmented reflexes or combat systems from activating.

Elena lay on the wet concrete, shaking. Not the full-body convulsion of the shock itself, but the aftershocks—small, violent tremors that rippled through her muscles as they tried to recalibrate after being overwhelmed. Her chest was heaving now, each breath a raw, ragged gasp as her respiratory muscles resumed function. Tears streamed from her eyes—partly from pain, partly from the involuntary irritation of the lacrimal glands during the shock, partly from grief.

Her chest, where the arc had struck, showed a small, shallow burn mark—a branching, fern-like pattern called a Lichtenberg figure, where the current entered the skin. The skin there was reddened and blistered at the center. Around it, the superficial capillaries in the skin had ruptured from the current's heat, leaving faint red lines that looked almost decorative, like a scar in the shape of a frozen lightning bolt.

Her muscles continued to spasm intermittently—twitches in her legs, a jerk in her left arm, a flutter in her jaw that made her teeth chatter involuntarily. These were the lingering neurological aftereffects. The motor neurons, still firing in the aftermath of the external stimulus, needed time to settle.

Kael knelt beside her. He checked her pulse—rapid, thready, but present. Her pupils were reactive. She was conscious.

"Elena," he said. "You're alive. Stay still. Don't try to move."

She looked up at him with eyes that held no rage now—only a vast, hollow exhaustion.

"The prototypes," she whispered. Her voice was shredded, raw from the scream she couldn't produce. "They're in my apartment. Sub-level 4, Building 97. I tagged the case with a dead-man's code. If I don't deactivate it in... fourteen hours... the data deletes itself."

"I'll make sure it gets recovered."

"And the story? Will anyone hear the story?"

Kael hesitated. The rain dripped through the broken ceiling of the service level, spattering on the concrete around them.

"I don't know," he said. And then, quietly: "But I'll tell it."

He pulled her to her feet—gently, one arm under her shoulders. She could barely stand. Her legs were rubbery and uncoordinated, muscles still misfiring from the neuromuscular trauma. He half-carried her to the service level exit, where his vehicle—a matte-black tactical skimmer—waited with its engine purring.

He eased her into the passenger seat and wrapped her in a thermal blanket. Her body temperature had dropped noticeably during the shock—electrical current can disrupt thermoregulation—and the trembling hadn't stopped.

As he guided the skimmer up through the rain toward the upper levels and the detention facility on Ward 7, Kael Voss looked at the woman shivering in his passenger seat. Forty-two thousand credits. That's what he'd been paid to bring her in. Enough to clear his debts and fund the next contract.

He thought about neural-interface prototypes and controlled-compliance hardware and a world where people's own implants could be used to make them obey.

He thought about how she'd stopped to eat a bowl of noodles before the end.

The rain kept falling. It smeared the neon further.

It never washed anything clean.

END

# The Weight of the Razor

The first thing Daniel noticed was the cold.

It crept through the thin fabric of his clothes like water, settling into his skin until it felt like part of him. The second thing he noticed was the weight.

His right arm — from shoulder to fingertips — was sealed inside a sleek metal casing shaped to the exact contour of his limb. It sat flush against a tabletop, anchored by bolts he could feel radiating faint vibrations through the steel. A faint hiss of pressurized gas bled from a seam near his wrist.

Above him, a monitor clicked on with a flicker of static.

The face that appeared was familiar in the worst way. That painted smile. The eyes that regarded suffering with something uncomfortably close to pedagogy.

"Hello, Daniel."

His own breathing was deafening in the silence.

"You've spent thirty-seven years avoiding responsibility. Avoiding pain. Avoiding every difficult choice by simply walking away. You walked away from your mother's bedside when she needed you. You walked away from your daughter when she pleaded with you to stay. You walked away from every hard thing, because the hard thing *scared* you."

Daniel's mouth worked but produced no sound.

"Today, you will not walk away."

The screen cut to a diagram. Inside the metal casing — which he could now see through a viewing window along its length — the mechanism was clearly displayed: his forearm, vulnerable and exposed in a narrow channel, sat beneath a perfectly sharpened blade that would retract unless a counterweight on the opposite side of the table was raised. That counterweight, he saw with a lurch of nausea, was a second channel — this one containing his *left* hand.

A handwritten note, laminated and placed just beyond the reach of his feet:

**"One hand holds the blade. The other is the lock. Sever your left hand at the wrist to release the mechanism and open the case. If both hands remain inside when the timer reaches zero, the gas will flood the case and the room. You have sixty seconds after the timer begins. The timer begins when you pick up the blade."**

Beneath the table, bolted to the edge within reach of his right hand if he contorted just so — because the case itself couldn't be opened or moved without releasing the mechanism — lay a retractable box cutter. Its blade was no more than an inch long.

Daniel stared at it.

His first response was disbelief. Not at the trap — he'd seen enough, heard enough, to know this was real. But at the *math* of it. An inch-long blade. A human wrist. His own left hand. The clean geometry of it was obscene in its simplicity. It wasn't a question of whether he *could* do it. It was a question of whether he could make his body cooperate with what his mind already knew.

*Thirty-six years and eleven months.*

The phrase surfaced from somewhere deep, unbidden. That was how old he'd be in two days. His birthday. His daughter had texted him just last week — *Happy almost birthday, Dad* — and he hadn't responded. He'd meant to. He'd meant to do a lot of things.

"Start now or don't start at all," he whispered to himself. The words tasted like nothing. His voice sounded like a stranger's.

He reached — slowly, his right arm nearly free of the case — and wrapped his fingers around the box cutter. The plastic was smooth and cold and impossibly light.

*Beep.*

The monitor flashed to a countdown. Sixty seconds.

Then forty-five. Then thirty.

He stared at his left hand.

It was *his* hand. The knuckles he'd cracked obsessively in law school. The callus on the middle finger from twenty years of gripping a pen. The slightly crooked pinky from a childhood fall. He could feel it — warm and pulsing and *alive* — pressed into the channel beneath the blade. His fingers twitched involuntarily, and he watched the tendons dance beneath the skin with a detachment that terrified him.

*I can't do this.*

*I can to do this.*

*I can't.*

His heartbeat was a war drum. The cold of the table had given way to something burning — not in his hand, but in his chest, spreading outward like a slow wildfire. Adrenaline. His body was already preparing for what his mind was refusing to authorize.

He thought of his daughter. Maya. Eight years old, with her mother's green eyes and a laugh that could stop traffic. The last thing she'd said to him — really said, with feeling — had been through tears in a hallway: *"Why do you always leave?"*

He thought of his mother. The way she'd squeezed his hand — this hand, this left hand — in the hospital. How he'd felt her grip weaken over three days. How he'd been holding it when she died and had never been able to explain why, for weeks afterward, he couldn't use a fork.

And he realized, with a clarity that felt like being struck, that he was about to lose this hand for the *right* reason. Maybe the first time in his life he'd endure something hard — not to walk away, but to reach *toward* something.

His fingers tightened on the box cutter.

Twelve seconds.

He placed the blade against the inside of his left wrist. The skin dimpled. He could feel his own pulse hammering against the metal — a frantic, confused rhythm, as if his body was trying to communicate a message his brain had already stopped listening to.

*This is not a negotiation,* he told himself.

*This is a door.*

His jaw clenched so hard his molars creaked. His eyes burned — not with tears, but with the sheer, primal effort of overriding every survival instinct that was *screaming* at him to stop. Every cell in his body begged. Pleaded. Negotiated.

He thought about walking away.

*You always walk away.*

Eight seconds.

The blade bit in.

The sound that came out of him wasn't a scream — it was something older than screaming. A noise from the bottom of the throat, from the animal underneath the man. His right hand shook so violently he had to use his thumb to brace it against the case. Blood — dark and immediate — welled around the blade and ran in warm rivulets down between his fingers, pooling in the channel.

Five seconds.

*Don't stop. If you stop now, she was right. Every time she said you don't have it in you. Don't stop.*

He bore down. The blade caught on something — bone, tendon, something structural and stubborn — and he made a sound that was not human, and he *twisted*, and felt something separate with a wet, dull pop, and the world went white and then red and then quiet.

*Beep.*

The case hissed. Pressurized air rushed out. The blade above his forearm retracted with a mechanical whisper.

Daniel slumped against the table, breathing in shallow, ragged gasps. His left arm ended in a ruin of blood and tissue just above the wrist. The hand was still inside the case. He couldn't look at it. He couldn't look away from it.

The monitor switched off.

In the silence, he became aware of a sound he hadn't registered before — a door, somewhere behind him, slowly grinding open on rusted hinges. Cool air moved across his face.

He didn't move. Not yet. He sat with the absence in his lap — with the *new* weight of it — and let it settle into him like the cold had settled in when he first woke up.

Then, slowly, he stood.

He left the box cutter on the table. He left the hand behind. He walked toward the door on legs that felt like someone else's, leaving a trail of red on the concrete.

His left arm throbbed with every heartbeat. Pain, like a second pulse. *Present. Alive. In this.*

He thought: *I'm not walking away.*

And for the first time in thirty-seven years, he meant it.

# The Plank

The noon sun turned the Caribbean to hammered gold, but for Silas Greaves, the light felt like an accusation.

Captain Evangeline Blackwood stood at the railing of *The Oathbreaker*, her tricorn hat casting a sharp shadow across the pale scars that traced her jaw. Her crew — the loyal ones, which now meant *all* of them again — formed a silent corridor along the starboard deck. Cutlasses gleamed. Eyes were hard.

"Silas." Her voice carried without effort. It always did. "You swore an oath on this deck. You broke it. Simple as that."

Silas's wrists burned where the rough hemp bit into them as two of Blackwood's enforcers shoved him forward. His knees nearly buckled. Behind him, the quartermaster — a broad woman named Nadia who had once been his friend — laid a weathered plank of teak across the gap between the ship's railing and a support beam, cantilevered out over open water. It groaned gently as it settled into place.

"Captain, please—" His voice cracked. He sounded like a boy. "I was going to return the share. I swear it—"

"You swore plenty," Blackwood said. She hadn't raised her voice. That was worse than shouting. "You were going to slip away at Tortuga with coin that belongs to sixty souls on this vessel. You put a knife to the throat of Old Maren when she caught you in the hold. *Old Maren*. Who bandaged your wounds at Nassau when you were too sick to stand."

Silas had no answer. The ropes binding his wrists were cut free, and he stumbled forward. The first plank beneath his bare feet was warm from the sun — strangely gentle, like stepping onto a porch in a quiet afternoon. The sea breeze lifted his hair. Somewhere above, a gull cried.

Then he looked down.

The water was a deep, luminous green-blue, impossibly clear in the shallow shelf off the reef. He could see fifteen feet down, maybe twenty. And what he saw made every muscle in his body go rigid.

Sharks.

Not one. Not two. A *shiver* of them — at least five — gliding in slow, lazy ellipses in the water below. Their grey-white forms moved with that terrible, unhurried economy of creatures who had never in their evolutionary history needed to rush. Hammerheads, he thought, or reef sharks — he didn't know, didn't care. What he knew was their *patience*. They circled in overlapping arcs, their pectoral fins cutting small wakes on the surface of their world. Occasionally one would break the pattern, surging upward, and for a flickering moment Silas would see the dark comma of its mouth and the pale, blank eye that held no malice and no mercy — only appetite.

The largest of them — a great dusky shape at least ten feet in length — paused directly beneath the plank. Its tail moved once, twice, holding it in place. Silas stared at its dorsal fin as it broke the surface and then slipped back under, sending a thin ring of ripple outward.

"We been trailing chum over the side since dawn," muttered one of the crew near the rail. A woman's voice, matter-of-fact. "Captain's orders."

Silas understood now. They hadn't just been lucky enough to encounter these creatures. Blackwood had *called* them. Had bled barrels of fish guts and chicken parts into the water for hours, staining the sea a faint pinkish brown, building the congregation below.

His feet moved forward on the plank, and the wood answered with a hollow, resonant *thunk*. Two steps. Three. The deck fell away behind him. The gap of open water between the plank's end and the sea spread wide — or perhaps it was just his vertigo making it seem so. The plank dipped slightly under his weight. Beneath it, the great dark shape turned, circling again, and Silas could see its ghostly white underbelly rotate like a page turning.

"Don't look down," Nadia said. Then, softer, almost a whisper: "God forgive me."

*She doesn't want this either*, Silas thought. *But she won't stop it. None of them will.*

Four steps. Five. The plank was a finger's width narrower than his feet, and his balance had always been poor. The breeze picked up and pushed at his chest, nudging him. A gull swooped low, inches from his head, and he flinched — felt the board sway beneath him — and his arms pinwheeled. The crew behind him went silent. Even the rigging seemed to hold its breath.

Below, the sharks surged. They *knew*. Some ancient sense — pressure change, vibration through the water — had told them that a meal was drawing closer. The lazy circles tightened into a tightening gyre. Five became eight, as more grey shapes materialized from the deep green gloom, rising up from below like lanterns in a dark hall. Their crescent tails churned the water into a froth of whitecaps around the ship's hull.

The largest shark — the captain of *that* vessel — rolled to the surface, and this time Silas saw the mouth. Rows of serrated, triangular teeth. A pale, terrible grin below the dark waterline. It hung there for a heartbeat, mouth slightly agape, and then it dropped back into the current and resumed its watch from below.

Silas's knees were shaking so badly the plank trembled. Tears slid down his cheeks and dropped into the ocean, joining the chum.

"Captain— *please*—"

"Six steps," Blackwood called. Her voice was level. Impersonal. Like reading a ledger. "You've got about three more before you reach the end. The sea will have you before I do."

"Give me another chance—"

"You *had* another chance. At Nassau. You spent it on drink and lies."

Silas squeezed his eyes shut. The sun pressed hot on his face. The sound of the water was enormous now — the slap and suck of it against the hull, the hiss of bubbles where the sharks churned below. He could *smell* the blood and chum rising up in warm, coppery waves. One of the sharks breached — a brief, violent eruption of spray and grey muscle — and the crew let out a collective grunt of surprise before falling silent again.

He opened his eyes. The end of the plank was one foot away. Below it, they waited. Eight… ten… he'd lost count. A living wheel of teeth and tail turning in the space between salvation and nothing.

"Evangeline—" He used her first name. It was the only card he had left.

She said nothing. The silence was the answer.

Silas looked at the water one final time. The largest shark was right below him now, so close that he could see the network of scars along its flank, the small remora fish clinging to its belly like parasites to a ruin. It turned its blunt head toward him and rose, rising, rising, the pale underbelly yawning open below him like a door—

He stepped off.

The plank clattered against the hull as his weight released it. For one half-second he was airborne, arms outstretched, the whole blue-green world spread beneath him — and then the water took him, and the cold was absolute, and the darkness closed over his head, and the last sound he heard was the roaring churn of hungry, indifferent mouths.

Above him, on the deck of *The Oathbreaker*, Captain Evangeline Blackwood removed her hat and pressed it against her heart. She looked at the pink-tinged water where the surface was still roiling and said, to no one in particular:

"So the oath holds."

Then she turned back to her crew.

"Now. Who wants to drink?"

# The Weight of Seconds

---

The first thing Daniel noticed was the weight.

It sat against his sternum like a second heartbeat — solid, dense, wrong. He'd felt it pressing through his shirt for the last several minutes, but he'd assumed it was a bruise, a soreness left over from sleeping awkwardly. Now, standing in the dim hallway, his fingers had pulled open his collar, and the fluorescent light had caught on something that was emphatically not a bruise.

A circuit board. Grey adhesive. Black casing — hard, curved to sit flush against him. And wires.

So many wires.

His fingertips hovered just above the surface, trembling, not quite touching. One hand pressed flat against the thing instead, fingers splayed, feeling its impossible *reality* through the pads of his skin. It was cool against his chest — cooler than body temperature — and its edges were sharp where the casing met the adhesive strips that bound it to him like a medical tape. He could feel the adhesive pulling at his chest hair, at his skin, every tiny shift of his breathing tugging at those bonds.

*Tick.*

His hand flinched.

*Tick.*

A small LED blinked red against the circuit board. Each flash was preceded by a click — not a clock's soft, round ticking but something thinner, hollower. Like a finger tapping a glass jar. *Tick. Tick.* The sound barely filled the hallway, yet it drowned out everything else.

*Tick.*

Daniel's breath went ragged. His fingers were moving now — not from choice — tracing the wires with the sickening attention of a man trying to understand what was killing him. The first wire was insulated in red rubber, thin as a headphone cord, running from the circuit board toward his left side, disappearing around the edge of the casing. The second was thinner still — a bare copper strand, its surface rough under his fingertip, slightly green with oxidation where it met a connector. It seemed to pulse. It wasn't pulsing. He *knew* it wasn't pulsing.

But he felt it anyway.

His finger caught on a third wire — black, wider, running along the underside. Where it pressed against his bare skin beneath the shirt, it was warm from his own heat, slick with a thin film of sweat. The texture made his stomach roll. Like touching something alive.

"Don't move," he whispered to himself, though no one was near.

*Tick.*

His fingers found the adhesive again — the strips that held it to him — and he *pulled*. Just a centimeter. The sensation of it separating from his skin was awful: a slow, tacky *release*, the glue stretching into thin threads, hair pulling, the skin beneath going red and screaming with a dull, spreading burn. Then the adhesive gave a gentle resistance — the wire was *taut*, anchored somewhere he couldn't see, threaded beneath the casing and around his torso like a harness. Pulling meant tugging that wire meant —

*Tick.*

He stopped.

His hand fell to his side, fingers still sticky with residue.

The hallway seemed to contract around him. The fluorescent light was buzzing — or was that just his ears? His heart was a war drum, and the thing against his chest rose and fell with each panicked breath, a terrible mirror of his own body. He could feel it through every nerve. The rigid board. The raised bumps of solder points catching on the fabric of his shirt like gravel. The cold central mass that he now realized was slightly convex, domed — shaped to hold something *inside* it.

Something that was not supposed to be inside anything.

His vision swam. He pressed his back against the wall and slid down it, his legs giving out with the fluidity of a puppet cut free. The device dug into his chest as he hit the floor, and he gasped — not from pain but from the *intimacy* of it, the way it molded to him as he curled inward. The wires shifted against his skin. One snagged on his nipple, and he let out a sound that was half laugh, half sob.

*Tick. Tick. Tick.*

Was it faster?

He pressed both hands against the casing — flat, desperate, as if he could hold it all together with pressure. His palms were slick. His fingertips found the thin copper wire again and followed it toward his back, where it split into a Y, one branch disappearing around his left side, the other angling toward his right. The junction was wrapped in black electrical tape, rough and ridged under his thumb. He could feel the two wires branching inside it like a forked tongue.

His breath became a pant. A sound escaped his throat — thin, involuntary, humiliating.

*Tick.*

He pulled at his shirt collar again, trying to see, tears blurring the blinking red light into a smear of color. The adhesive on one strip had begun to fail, the edge curling, and the thing shifted on his chest by a quarter inch — an ocean of movement — and every hair on his body stood on end.

*It could go off with movement. It could go off with tampering. It could go off because it's been sixty seconds since the last —*

*Tick.*

The LED pulsed.

Daniel's hands found his face. His fingers pressed into his eye sockets until stars burst, and he squeezed, and he *rocked*, and the thing on his chest moved with him like a barnacle, like a parasite, like a second heart he had never agreed to grow. The wires were everywhere — he could feel them in his imagination spreading like roots through his ribcage, wrapping his lungs, threading through his bones.

*Tick.*

His mouth opened and a sound came out — raw, guttural, the kind of sound he'd never made in his life. It echoed off the hallway walls and came back to him doubled, as if the building were laughing.

*Tick.*

He was going to die strapped to a circuit board and copper wire and the sound of his own countdown.

*Tick.*

His fingers, wet with tears and sweat, found one last wire — far right, barely insulated, so thin it felt like a thread of spider silk against the pad of his index finger. And he held it. Because what else could he do? He held the thinnest wire like a lifeline, and his chest heaved, and the LED blinked red in time with something that was not his heart but claimed to be.

*Tick.*

The hallway stretched on.

The light buzzed.

The wire waited.

# Still Water

The sound woke her — not a crash or a bang, just the soft, wrong sound of something settling inside the house that didn't belong to her.

Elena's eyes opened in the dark of the bedroom. She lay rigid, the sheet tangled around one hip, her breath held somewhere in her throat. The ceiling above her was a wash of gray-black. The numbers on the nightstand clock read 3:14 AM.

*Probably nothing. The old wood expands and contracts. It's August. The house is just breathing.*

She heard it again. A faint, careful shift of weight. A floorboard somewhere on the first floor — the long one near the kitchen doorway, the one that always groaned.

Someone was standing on it.

Elena sat up slowly, dragging the sheet with her out of some nameless instinct, as if cotton could protect her. Her phone was in the kitchen. She'd plugged it into the charger before bed and told herself she'd grab it in the morning. The landline was in the hallway — but she hadn't paid that bill in three months and the line was dead.

She pressed her feet to the floor. The hardwood was warm from the August night, and the feeling of it against her bare soles made everything too real.

*Call out. Say something. "Hello?" Like an idiot in a movie.*

She didn't call out.

The hallway stretched out before her like a dark hallway, which is exactly what it was. The bathroom door was closed on the left. The guest room on the right was empty — no door even, just an open arch, nothing but her grandmother's old dresser inside. At the end, the staircase descended into a black mouth.

She moved to the wall and trailed her fingers along the drywall as she walked. Each step was placed with the exaggerated care of someone stepping on ice. Her palm found the doorframe at the top of the stairs and she gripped it.

Below, in the dark, someone shifted their weight again.

She could hear it now — could hear *them*. Breathing. Slow and controlled. Measured. The breathing of someone who wasn't scared. Someone who was doing this on purpose.

Every instinct in Elena's body screamed at her to retreat. Close the bedroom door. Push the dresser against it. Scream until a neighbor called the police.

He wasn't running.

He was walking.

He knew she had nowhere to go.

# Trench 7 — No Man's Land, 1916

The canister coughed its answer across the parapet before anyone could cry out.

First came the smell — sharp, metallic, like a struck match shoved into the mouth. It wasn't the gas that did the most damage at first. It was the panic. The men who ripped their hoods off too late. The ones whose fingers wouldn't tie the strings. The ones who understood, in the space of one ragged inhale, that something had changed in the chemical composition of their own lungs.

---

**The Physical:**

His throat closed as though an invisible fist had seized the column of his neck from inside and twisted. Every breath became a negotiation — a desperate, strangled bargain with muscles that had seized and spasmed. He wheezed, and the sound that came out was not human. It was a reed — a cheap, broken pipe played by something that had forgotten what music was. High, thin, reedy. Each exhalation squealed. Each inhalation dragged over tissue that felt as though it were being peeled apart with a dull knife.

The cough came in convulsions. Not polite, controllable coughs — but seizure-like convulsions that bent him double at the waist and drove his forehead into the mud wall of the trench. His diaphragm seized, released, seized again. Each spasm pulled fresh vapor deeper into the bronchial tree. He felt it travel — felt the clawing sensation migrate from throat to trachea to bronchi and then settle into the soft, spongy tissue of the lungs themselves like fire soaking into a wet rag, smoldering from within.

His chest burned. Not the surface — deeper. Behind the ribs. Behind the sternum. It felt as though someone had poured hot lye directly into the alveoli and there was no valve to close, no way to un-exhale it back out. He pressed his hands against his sternum as if he could physically push the pain out, or push air in. It did neither.

His eyes streamed — not from emotion but from the chemical tearing the corneal epithelium. They swelled shut. The skin around them puffed and glistened. Everything beyond arm's reach became a blur of brown mud and gray light and the silhouettes of men who were also bending, also curling, also making that awful reedy sound.

His lips turned a dull cyanotic blue. The fingertips followed. His body was starving for oxygen in the middle of the shallowest, smallest space on earth.

Mucus flooded from his nose and mouth — thick, yellowish, threaded with red where the capillaries had burst. He coughed and something heavier came up. Something with weight to it. He didn't look down. He already knew.

His legs gave way. He sat in the mud and the puddle of standing water at the bottom of the trench, and he could not stand, and he could not think of standing, because every single ounce of his neurological capacity was devoted to one task: breathe. Just breathe. One more time. One more time.

---

**The Mental:**

There is a moment in the mind before the body fully understands — a terrible, suspended half-second in which the brain *knows* but the self has not yet accepted. He was there. He stood in that half-second. The thought was crystalline and absurd in its simplicity: *This is actually happening to me.*

Then the panic arrived like a second wave of gas.

It was not the gas that frightened him anymore. It was the sound of his own breathing — that thin, reedy, childish whine. He heard himself sounding like something pathetic and small, and it offended some deep, animal part of him. He wanted to scream but screaming meant opening his mouth wider and drawing in more.

He thought of his mother. Not with tenderness — with rage. With the specific, helpless fury of a child who has been hurt and cannot tell anyone. *I want my mother.* The thought was disgusting to him and he clung to it anyway.

He thought of nothing. The mind, past a certain threshold of suffering, goes quiet. Not peaceful — *vacant*. Like a house after the family has been dragged out of it. The lights are off. The chairs are still warm. There is no one home.

He prayed. He did not believe in God and had not believed in God since a farmhouse in Picardy eleven months ago, but he prayed the way a drowning man grabs at water — instinctively, futilely, with both hands.

And then the breathing, which had been his only task, his only thought, his only reason for existing in this mud trench at the bottom of the world — the breathing became *quieter*. Not because he was getting better. Because the inflamed tissue was swelling shut. The airway was closing. The narrow pipe through which life traveled was being pinched by his own body's damage.

He felt it. The quietness. And he understood it.

He did not scream. He did not have the air to scream.

---

The medic found him forty minutes later, propped against the trench wall with his hood around his neck and his mouth open and his eyes swollen shut and that awful reedy sound still — *still* — coming from somewhere deep in the wreckage of his chest. The medic knelt beside him and did not touch him, because there was nothing to touch, and said nothing, because there was nothing to say.

The sound eventually stopped.

# Paperwork

The office smelled of espresso and old leather. Vito Moretti didn't look up from the ledger when Rocco stepped through the door.

"The books balanced?"

"Yes, Don Moretti." Rocco kept his hands clasped behind his back. "Everything checks out. Except one entry."

Now Vito looked up. His reading glasses caught the lamplight. "Which entry?"

"Serrano. Last week's shipment to the docks. Two hundred thousand in transit. He signed for all of it." Rocco paused. "One hundred and fifty arrived at the warehouse."

Silence. Vito removed his glasses and polished them with a silk cloth, one slow circle, then another. He set them neatly on the desk.

"And where do you think the rest went?"

"His wife bought a house in Boca last Tuesday. Cash."

Vito nodded slowly, as though Rocco had told him something about the weather. He stood and walked to the window. The city glowed below like a carpet of embers.

"I brought him in when he was sixteen years old," Vito said quietly. "He used to shine my shoes at this very desk." He let out a breath that wasn't quite a sigh. "Send him to the accountant."

Rocco's jaw tightened almost imperceptibly. "The accountant will need to conduct a full audit. I understand."

"That's right. A *very* thorough audit. Have Gianni and Petey assist. They're good with numbers." Vito paused. "Make sure nothing is left on the books afterward. Clean up the paperwork completely. He won't be filing any more reports."

"And the family?"

"His wife can keep the house in Boca. Call it a severance package." Vito turned back to the window. "She has the children to think about."

Rocco inclined his head. "When would you like the meeting?"

"Soon. Tomorrow, before he starts his shift." Vito reached up and straightened a small crucifix on the wall. "Have him come to the old warehouse on 9th. Tell him there's a discrepancy to resolve. He'll come. He always wants to explain himself."

"And if he brings anyone?"

"Don't worry about that." Vito settled back into his chair and opened the ledger to a fresh page. "Gianni and Petey will handle any... loose ends. The accountant is very efficient when he's not working alone."

Rocco stood motionless a moment longer. "He was loyal for eleven years, Don Moretti."

Vito's pen scratched against paper. "He was *paid* for eleven years. That's not the same thing." He didn't look up. "Is there anything else?"

"No, Don Moretti."

"Then go. And Rocco — make sure the accountant's final report is clean. No witnesses, no leftovers. Afterward, I want to hear that he simply... moved on. Retired early. Took a vacation he never came back from." Vito's voice carried no more weight than a man reciting a grocery list. "We don't like unpleasant endings in this family."

Rocco nodded once and turned toward the door.

"And Rocco."

He stopped.

"Send flowers to his wife on my behalf. White lilies."

The door clicked shut. Vito made another entry in the ledger, the strokes precise and even, and the office returned to the quiet rustle of turning pages.

# The Weight of Earth

# The Rematch

The ring smelled like copper and old sweat.

Dino Marchetti's left eye had sealed shut by the fourth round, the lid swollen to the size of a plum, the skin stretched tight and shiny as a grape about to burst. His right eye wasn't much better — the sclera was now half-crimson, blood seeping from a cut along the brow ridge and pooling in the socket until every blink sent a thin red film sliding across his vision. The world had gone to soft, rust-tinted shapes. He couldn't see the ropes anymore. He could only see Marcus "The Scythe" Ward coming toward him in red haze, a blurry mountain of motion.

Another right cross connected. The sound was wet — leather and knuckle compressing against already-ruined tissue. Dino's nose let out a spray of blood and cartilage fragments that misted the front row. He felt the bridge of it shift sideways, still attached but no longer where it belonged. Something was grinding in there now when he breathed.

He tried to keep his guard up but his arms had gone to lead. His elbows felt like they were on a half-second delay from his brain. His ribs told him why. Round after round of body shots had turned his midsection into a swollen wreck — the left side was visibly distended now, one rib already cracked and moving in ways no bone should move when he exhaled. He could feel it grinding, a subtle sickening *click-click* between breaths, pain lighting up his whole torso like a fuse.

Then the right hand came again.

Ward dug a short uppercut beneath the elbow — surgical, vicious, exactly where the damage already lived. Dino heard it before he felt it.

*Crack.*

Not the pop of a glove against flesh. Not the familiar thud of a liver shot. This was dry and hollow and *definitive* — the sound of calcified bone fracturing along a fracture line, like a green branch snapping over someone's knee. It echoed in the marrow of his skull. The broken rib — or what had been the cracked one — had now split clean, the jagged ends shearing apart and driving into the intercostal muscle between them.

Dino's legs didn't buckle. They simply stopped receiving instructions.

He slumped forward into Ward's chest, not from strategy, not from clinching, but because gravity finally won. Ward pushed him off and stepped back as the referee stepped in — or tried to. But Dino was already going down on his own, folding sideways, the mat rising up to meet his face.

He landed on his ruined ribcage and screamed. The sound came out garbled through the blood in his mouth — he'd swallowed so much it was pooling in his stomach now, heavy and nauseating. His left eye was nothing but a sealed purple bruise. His right eye, swimming in blood, looked up at the lights through the crimson film, and for one terrible moment he could see Ward standing over him — arms raised, jaw working on the mouthpiece, not even breathing hard.

The referee's face floated into view. Ten fingers held up. They blurred together. Dino couldn't count them.

He wasn't sure anyone could.
