# The Sentence

The courtyard fell silent. A silence that felt weighted, manufactured — the kind that presses against the eardrums like deep water.

Marcus stood at the post with his wrists bound above his head, the coarse hemp already chafing raw circles around his bones. He was facing the weathered grain of the oak, but he could feel the crowd behind him — hundreds of soldiers and citizens drawn to the spectacle of imperial justice, a word that struck him now as the cruelest kind of joke.

Centurion Draeco moved into position behind him. Marcus heard the whip uncoil, heard the thick leather whisper against the flagstones as its handler let it out to full length — eight feet of braided rawhide tipped with a knotted strand of horsehair.

"You have been sentenced to twenty-five lashes," Draeco announced to the silent courtyard, though his voice was directed at Marcus. "For the crime of sedition."

Marcus closed his eyes.

The first blow came without warning.

There was a sound — a sharp, wet *crack*, like a tree branch snapping in ice, but with something beneath it, something fleshy and wrong. The knot of the lash struck between his shoulder blades and the world became white for a moment. He felt the skin part before he felt the pain, a bright, shearing line that opened along his back as though someone had drawn a red-hot blade across him. The rawhide bit deep and then dragged, tearing along the wound as it pulled away, and Marcus heard — actually *heard* — the sound of his own flesh tearing, a faint, wet sound like canvas being ripped. Then the pain arrived, rushing in from both ends of the wound to meet in the middle and detonate.

He gasped. His knuckles whitened on the post.

A murmur rippled through the crowd.

The second lash fell before his breath had fully returned. This one crossed the first at an angle, lower, just above the hip, and the knot caught on the ridge of his spine before it dragged sideways. He felt the skin split in a jagged gash, felt the edge of the wound curl slightly outward as it opened, and the blood followed immediately — warm and sudden, already running in thin rivulets toward the waistband of his ragged trousers. The sound of the tearing was smaller this time, drowned by his own cry, a hoarse, involuntary bark of agony that he bit off halfway through.

*One. Two.*

He counted. It was the only thing he had.

The third lash struck the same territory as the first, landing just beside the initial wound, and he felt the skin near the old cut give way with almost no resistance at all — it was already weakened, already compromised — and the lash went deeper than before. The knot carved through to the tissue beneath the dermis, and the sound it made was less a crack and more a dull, muffled thud, the kind of sound a chisel makes when it bites into soft wood. The skin tore in long, curling strips along the trajectory of the blow, and for one impossible instant, Marcus could feel the air moving across the exposed meat of the wound, cool and obscene against the inside of himself.

His legs buckled. The hemp bit into his wrists and held him upright.

Draeco swung again.

*Four.*

The lash landed on his side this time, wrapping around the rib cage, and it took a strip of skin from his flank with it, leaving behind a narrow, pale crescent where the flesh had simply been peeled away from the muscle beneath. Blood flooded the wound instantly, almost black in the cold light. He heard it spatter against the flagstones — *plock, plock* — small sounds, like rain on stone.

The crowd was no longer silent. They murmured now, shifting, some leaning forward. Marcus could hear their breathing.

*Five. Six.*

Blows fell in the same region, each one landing on damaged tissue, each one opening the wounds wider. The sound of the lash had changed by the tenth strike — what had started as a crisp, clean *crack* was now a wet, glutinous sound, like leather striking a soaked rag, because there was so much blood on his back now that the whip could no longer find dry skin to tear. It simply opened what was already open, split the raw, red margins of the wounds, widened them by fractions of an inch each time. Small pieces of flesh — ragged, irregular, glistening — had begun to accumulate along the knots of the whip and fall away with each swing, dropping to the stones below.

*Twelve.*

"Keep his legs, if he falls," Draeco instructed the two soldiers at the post.

Marcus had lost the ability to cry out. His jaw ached from clenching. His vision swam. Each breath dragged across the inside of his rib cage and felt like swallowing glass. The air against his back was no longer cool — the exposed tissue radiated its own terrible warmth.

*Fifteen.*

He barely registered the sound anymore. Just a rhythm now, steady and mechanical. *Crack-thud. Crack-thud.* The tearing of skin had become a texture rather than a noise, woven into the percussion of the lash like a second instrument. The crowd had grown very quiet again, the way people grow quiet when the spectacle has moved past entertainment and into something they don't have language for.

*Twenty. Twenty-one.*

Something in the upper wound had given way entirely. A flap of skin — a strip an inch wide and nearly four inches long — hung loose from his back, swinging slightly with each breath he took, attached to him by only the blood-slicked margin at one end. He couldn't see it, but he could feel it moving, this terrible flag of his own body, and the sensation of it was somehow worse than the pain.

*Twenty-three.*

The crowd flinched.

*Twenty-four.*

The last lash fell with the same precise, practiced force as the first. It landed across the open hollow of his back where there was almost nothing left to cut, and the sound it made was soft — almost gentle — a faint, wet tear, like peeling the rind from an overripe fruit. The last resistance of ruined skin gave way, and the knot struck the dense, red muscle beneath with a muffled thud.

*Twenty-five.*

"Done," Draeco said.

Silence again, absolute.

Marcus stood bound to the post, breathing in shallow, broken sips. Blood ran from his shoulders to his ankles in a slow, continuous sheet, collecting in dark pools at his bare feet. His back was no longer recognizable as a surface of skin — it was a geography of open, weeping wounds, strips of torn flesh hanging in ragged petals, the pale yellow of exposed fat visible along the deepest cuts. Flies were already arriving, drawn by the smell.

He did not fall.

He would not fall.

# The First Bite

The cold had stopped being something they felt and started being something they *were*. Seven days. Maybe eight—Ren had lost the thread of counting somewhere around the third, when the sun came out briefly and then the whiteout swallowed them again.

She could no longer feel her fingers when she reached for the water. The boiled snow left a taste of nothing, a cold emptiness that reminded her stomach it was eating itself.

There were four of them left. Dan, who'd broken both legs in the crash and hadn't spoken since the second day. Lisette, who'd wrapped her sleeping bag around Dan and was shivering so hard now she'd stopped producing even that sound. Marcus, who kept looking at the fuselage wreckage like it held an answer.

And Ren.

The first body had been Mrs. Alderman. The flight attendant. She'd stopped breathing sometime in the night and Ren had known—*known*—before Lisette confirmed it, had felt the room of the tent get smaller and darker around the shape of the dead woman.

That was when it began. Not the act. The *argument*.

It started as a whisper. A suggestion so faint it felt like someone else's thought drifting through the dead air. It wore the voice of survival instinct—practical, clinical, almost kind. *There is a resource. You are not desecrating her. She is gone. This is chemistry and biology. Calories are fuel. You are a machine that will stop functioning without fuel.*

Ren pressed her palms against her face and breathed into her hands and tried to let the thought pass.

It did not pass.

It *settled*.

---



The argument was never between Ren and another person. It was between Ren and the architecture of being human. Somewhere deep in the synaptic plumbing of her consciousness, there was a wall. A load-bearing wall. And the thought was pressing against it with the slow, patient pressure of water finding a crack in stone.

*It's wrong*, she thought.

*Why?* asked the other voice. Not cruel. Not monstrous. Almost gentle. Almost reasonable. *Define 'wrong.' Wrong compared to what? Wrong compared to the two of you dying alongside two corpses and four dead limbs and a broken fuselage? Wrong is an abstraction. Right now, abstractions are a luxury you cannot afford.*

She thought about God. She thought about what her mother would say. She thought about how she would live with herself afterward.

*You will live with yourself afterward. That's the point. There is no 'afterward' without this.*

This was the psychological break—not a dramatic moment of madness but a quiet, structural failure. Like a bone that has been bearing weight past its limit and doesn't snap but instead *folds*, buckles inward, changes shape permanently. The wall didn't shatter. It simply stopped holding.

Ren didn't make a decision. Decisions are acts of will, and will requires a chooser, an intact self standing at a fork in a road. What happened instead was a *drift*. The self she had been—the one who cried at veterinary commercials and called her sister every Sunday and believed in fairness—that self quietly stepped backward into fog. It didn't die. It just... became someone she could set down like luggage she couldn't carry anymore.

*Set it down,* the voice said. *You can pick it up later. Maybe.*

---



Lisette was watching her. Lisette, who understood what the silence meant, who could see it in the way Ren's eyes kept drifting to the body and then snapping away and then drifting again, a compass needle fighting its alignment.

"We don't have to talk about it," Lisette said.

"I need to talk about it," Ren said. And then: "I need you to tell me it's okay."

Lisette's mouth opened and closed. The shivering made everything slower, like speaking through deep water.

"It's okay," Lisette whispered.

"That's not—" Ren stopped. "You don't mean that."

"No." Lisette pulled Dan's jacket tighter around her shoulders. "I mean—I don't know what I mean. I mean she would—"

"Don't say that. Don't say *she would want us to*. She wouldn't. That's a lie people tell to sleep."

Silence. The wind threw grit against the tent.

"Then what?" Lisette asked.

# The First Course

The metal plate clattered onto the table in front of Ethan, and for one horrible, crystalline moment, the room fell silent—just the hum of whatever machine powered this room, and the wet clicking sound from *them*.

The things on the plate were beetles. Dozens of them. Pale, fat larvae the size of his thumb, squirming over each other in a slick, translucent mass that glistened under the single dangling bulb. Mixed among them were dark, hard-shelled roaches, their legs twitching in broken loops. Everything was slicked with something oily and dark. Brine, maybe. Or soy sauce. Something meant to suggest that this was *food*.

The trap was simple in its cruelty. A metal helmet with a jaw-locking mechanism had been placed over his head and bolted to the chair at the neck. He could open his mouth, but only if he moved forward—toward the plate. Behind him, a counter readout displayed a weight sensor beneath the plate. Forty grams. He had to remove forty grams from the plate and swallow it. The timer above the door read *3:52... 3:51...*

A needle of coolant was aimed at the back of his neck from inside the collar of the helmet. The voice had explained: failure to comply before the timer reached zero would result in the injection of a neurotoxin. He had four minutes to decide between vomit and death.

"The spectacle is the point," the voice had said over the speakers. Its cadence was calm, almost professorial. "Survival requires the death of dignity. Let us begin."

Ethan leaned forward. The helmet's jaw-lock released with a click. His mouth opened—but his stomach was already climbing. The smell hit him from inches away: a thick, sour, deeply animal stench that coated the back of his throat like wet fur. It was the smell of something that had been *inside* something else. His eyes watered instantly.

*Pick them up. Pick. Them. Up.*

His fingers hovered over the mass. They were warm. The larvae pulsed beneath his fingertips with an internal peristalsis he could feel through his skin—a slow, muscular squirm, like palming a small living organ. One of the roaches scrambled over his knuckles, its legs pricking like pinheads, and he flinched so hard his arm struck the table.

The counter readout still read *0/40g*. The timer hit *3:22*.

He grabbed a fistful. The larvae burst between his fingers, releasing a hot, viscous gel that ran into his sleeve and down his wrist. It was the texture of a runny egg yolk mixed with warm gelatin. The smell doubled. A roach crunched loudly—audibly—between his middle and ring finger, and something wet and soft escaped the shell.

He opened his mouth.

The back of his throat locked. His gag reflex fired before anything had even entered his mouth—an involuntary full-body convulsion that clamped his stomach up through his diaphragm and made his vision swim. Saliva flooded his mouth in thick, hot waves. His body was already trying to evacuate.

*Thirty grams left. Just do it. Just—*

He shoved the handful in.

The texture was immediate and total. The larvae were slimy and soft, collapsing instantly against his tongue, releasing a bitter, ammonia-tasting fluid that seeped between his teeth. The roach shell sat on top of it—a hard, rubbery lump that his tongue tried desperately to push toward his lips. He could feel the individual legs against his palate, the jagged little hooks catching on his soft tissue like Velcro.

His throat refused. His esophagus pinched shut and his body jackknifed forward, the chair scraping across concrete as he retched. The contents of his mouth surged toward his lips, and he had to press his hand over his own mouth, forcing the liquid back down with the pressure of his palm. His nostrils flared. A strand of something drew a line between his lips and the plate.

The gooey residue coated every surface of his mouth. It tasted like wet soil and battery acid and something faintly, sweetly rotten—like fruit left in a car in summer. He could feel tiny pieces of leg riding on the film of slime on his tongue. He tried not to think about it. He swallowed.

The lump moved down his throat like a living thing, gripping at the walls of his esophagus, and he felt it enter his stomach with a warm, rolling nausea that radiated outward to his fingertips. His stomach rejected it immediately, and he dry-heaved violently, his throat burning with stomach acid. His eyes streamed.

The counter read *14/40g*.

*2:47.*

He looked at the plate again. The remaining larvae writhed in the oil-dark fluid. One was on its back, its tiny mouth-parts working uselessly at the air. The smell was in his nose now, clinging to the inside of his nostrils like tar. He knew it would be there for hours.

The voice spoke. "You're doing admirably."

Ethan reached back into the pile. His fingers sank to the second knuckle. This time he closed his fist and squeezed—trying to destroy the structure of the things before they reached his mouth. More larvae burst. The fluid was warm. It smelled stronger when the bodies were ruptured.

He brought his fist to his lips and didn't think.

He chewed.

The sound was obscene. Wet, compressive crunching and squelching that reverberated through the helmet. His molars ground through a roach shell—it shattered into shards that poked into his tongue and the inside of his cheek. Beneath it, the larval matter spread across his teeth and into the gaps between them like cold paste. His tongue involuntarily rolled the material, tasting every dimension of it—mold, salt, that horrible sweet rot, and underneath it all, something faintly metallic.

His body lurched. His stomach surged upward and he tasted his own acid, felt the mixture of larval paste and vomit boiling at the back of his mouth. He gagged again—a long, involuntary retch that made his whole body shake. For three agonizing seconds the mouthful sat at the threshold of his lips, and he pressed his fist to his mouth again and *pushed*.

He swallowed.

It went down wrong. The mass caught in his throat and he choked—real choking, his airway obstructed, his lungs seizing. He doubled over, eyes bulging, fingers clawing at the metal collar around his neck. The helmet held firm. For five terrible seconds he couldn't breathe, the bolus of crushed insects and larvae lodged in the back of his throat like a cork, and black dots swam across his vision.

Then it slid.

He vomited immediately—a violent, full-body spasm that emptied his stomach of whatever breakfast he'd eaten that morning and sent it all over the plate. The counter dipped to *9/40g* as the vomit displaced some of the remaining insects off the edge.

*1:34.*

His throat burned. His eyes burned. His nose was running, and he couldn't tell if it was mucus or the fluid from the larvae or both. His tongue was still working involuntarily against the residue in his mouth, and every time it moved, he tasted it again—*felt* it again—and his stomach clenched.

He grabbed the last handful. The plate scraped. The larvae were half-submerged in his own vomit now, and the smell had become something else entirely—something that didn't belong in any taxonomy of smell, that existed only in the overlap between sickness and putrefaction and hunger.

He stuffed the handful past his lips. He didn't chew this time. He tilted his head back and swallowed the mass whole—felt it draw down like a dying fish, slithering past his uvula and down into his stomach, where it landed in the ruin of what was already there.

The counter read *42/40g*.

A green light. The collar hissed and released. The helmet lifted. The voice spoke one final word:

"Appetizer."

The door to the next room unlocked.

Ethan fell off the chair and onto his hands and knees on the concrete, retching in long, dry heaves that produced only acid and bile. His fingers dug into the floor. He could still feel the legs on his palate. The legs, and the squirm, and the taste. He knew—with a certainty that lived in his bones now—he would never fully stop tasting it.

# The Rite of the Black Altar

The temple swallowed light.

Carved deep into the volcanic rock beneath a mountain that had not erupted in living memory, the chamber breathed like a lung — slow, sulfurous exhalations curling from fissures in the floor. Thousands of iron channels grooved the ceiling like the ribs of some enormous carcass, and along each one, black candles had been affixed in decades past with human fat. Their flames burned without warmth, the way stars burn across a void.

The floor was a mosaic. Under the coating of centuries of soot and dried offerings, it told a story — a spiral, widening and tightening, depicting the cycle the temple's builders understood the world to run upon: birth, feeding, death, and return. The spiral's center was occupied by the altar: a single slab of basalt, waist-high, pockmarked with channels cut purposefully at its lip so that whatever bled upon its surface would be captured and directed down into the earth below.

Beneath the altar, the ground was black with it. Decades. Centuries. Layered and fossilized.

# The Slow Return

The overhead light had become a suggestion.

Not gone — not yet — but reduced to an idea of brightness, the way a word remembered a hundred times loses its shape in the mouth. Elias blinked against it, and each blink was longer than the last, a shutter closing in half-degrees until the gaps between seeing stretched into something like sleep.

He'd stopped trying to move.

Somewhere behind the bar — he'd felt the ridge of it against his spine as he slid down — there were shelves of bottles he could no longer turn to look at. He didn't need to see them. He knew the order of things the way he'd known his own kitchen in the dark: whiskey here, whiskey beside it, the cheap stuff by the register where the good stuff used to be before everything kept changing.

The floor was cold.

Not at first. At first, after Donnelly's knife had opened him — that silver, silver flash in the bar light — he'd been warm. Furious warm. The kind of heat that makes you slam your fist against the ground and swear you'll *get up*, you'll get up right now, just give the blood a second to stop.

But blood doesn't stop just because you ask.

He felt it leaving him in slow intervals. A tide going out through the gaps in his ribs where the first wound was, where the second wound was — Donnelly had made him turn, made him stumble backward into the stool that knocked him down — and now there was a third thing happening that wasn't quite pain anymore but its older brother, *pressure*, a heavy, velvet thing that sat on his chest and wouldn't lift.

The cold came from underneath. From the tiles. From the ground claiming its share of him.

It crept up his arms first — a tingling that started at the wrists and climbed the long avenue of his forearms like something small and patient. Then his legs. Then his stomach, which had been the warmest part of him, the fire in the engine room, and now it was cooling like a stove turned off at midnight, still glowing but giving up the heat in long, slow breaths.

He pressed his hand to the wound. Felt the wet of himself through his shirt. It was the same warmth as tears, he thought. Or maybe that was just his body running out of better comparisons.

*Heartbeat.*

There it was. The one sound left.

He hadn't heard it at first. There had been the crash of the stool, the creak of the door as Donnelly left — that horrible, casual *creak* — and the distant sounds of the street: a car, a dog, a life continuing on the other side of the wall where people still had their blood and didn't know what a miracle it was to keep it.

But those sounds had thinned out. The dog went first. Then the car. Then the street itself became a concept, not a sound, and in the silence his heartbeat rose like a deep drum in an empty cathedral.

*Thoom. Thoom. Thoom.*

It was enormous now. Reverberating. He could feel it in his teeth, in the soft behind his eyes, in the place where his thoughts were slowly gathering at the edges of his awareness and then drifting apart again, like people at a party when the music stops.

*Thoom.*

*Thoom.*

Slower now. He noticed it slowing, the way you notice a train decelerating into the station — not suddenly but by degrees, each interval a half-beat longer than the last, the drum choosing its moments with a strange, reluctant dignity.

He thought of his mother's kitchen. Light through the window above the sink — yellow, late, the kind of light that says *dinner's almost ready* even if you can't smell anything yet. The light had the same quality as the one above him now, reduced and soft and turning orange at the edges. He watched it go and didn't try to keep it.

The cold had reached his chest.

His hand was still pressed to the wound, but he couldn't feel the wet anymore. He couldn't feel much at all. The pressure on his ribs had eased — his body giving up its argument one point at a time — and in its place was a stillness that didn't feel wrong. It felt like the bottom of a lake. Still and cold and absolute.

*Thoom.*

He waited for the next one. Counted in the way children count thunder: *one-Mississippi, two-Mississippi* — but slower than that. So much slower. The spaces between the beats were rooms now. Hallways. The beat would come, and then there would be a long, quiet corridor of nothing, and he would walk it alone and it would be all right and then there would be another beat and he would remember he had a body and it would be leaving.

*Thoom.*

The light was a candle.

He was sure of that now. Whatever it had been — fluorescent, halogen, the sad thin bulb over the bar that flickered on Tuesdays — it was a candle now. A single warm point above him, shrinking. The room had gone to edges and shadows, and beyond the shadows was the dark, and the dark was patient and had all the time in the world and was in no hurry to touch him.

He was cold to the chin now.

The heat of him was a small island somewhere near his throat, the last territory, the flag still flying over a city that had already fallen. He watched his hand on his chest and couldn't tell if it was still his hand. It looked like someone else's. It looked like it belonged to the tiles.

*Thoom.*

The candle flickered.

He closed his eyes. Behind them, his mother's kitchen was still there — the window, the light, the counters wiped clean. She was humming something. She was always humming something. The tune didn't matter. What mattered was the humming itself, the sound of being alive without thinking about it, the heart doing its work without asking for attention or thanks.

*Thoom.*

A beat so gentle it was almost silence.

*Thoo*—

The kitchen light went out.

Not all at once. The way dawn comes in reverse — gradually, in purples, in grays, in the soft black that isn't dark yet but is learning. He felt it as a warmth leaving his jaw, his mouth, the small muscles around his eyes. The last of him going to the floor, to the tiles, to whatever the ground keeps of us.

One more.

He waited for one more.

The drum was far away now. In another room. Another life. It would come or it wouldn't come and either way, the kitchen was quiet and the counters were clean and his mother had stopped humming and the house was still and the stillness was kind.

It didn't come.

It didn't need to.

The silence was warm at the very last. The cold was gone. The light was gone. The heartbeat was gone. And in the space where everything had been, there was a single, sustained note — not a sound but a feeling — like the last string on a guitar holding its pitch after the pluck, trembling through the body of the wood until the wood forgets what the note was and goes back to being wood.

Elias went back to being still.

The bar was quiet.

Outside, a dog barked. Then stopped. Then the street continued its long, unbothered breath.

# The Note on the Windowsill

The bedroom was too clean.

Detective Mara Kessler noticed it the moment she stepped through the doorway — the way every surface gleamed, the way the pillows on the twin bed sat at identical angles. A child's room that looked like a photograph of a child's room. No dust. No crumbs. No chaos.

A seven-year-old lived here. Or had.

The goldfish was in the small blue bowl on the dresser. Had been. Its body floated at an impossible angle, one eye toward the ceiling. A thin curl of something dark clouded the water. Kessler leaned in, then pulled back. The smell was faint but unmistakable — bleach. Just a few drops, maybe, carefully dosed.

She looked at the boy sitting in the hallway on a folding chair, knees drawn up, watching the forensics team with the patient curiosity of someone observing ants. Officer Brennan crouched beside him, speaking in that low, coaxing voice adults used when they wanted a child to feel safe.

He didn't look afraid.

"Eat your sandwich," Brennan was saying. "It's turkey. You like turkey, right?"

The boy — Jonah — said nothing. He chewed precisely, four times, then swallowed. His eyes tracked Kessler as she turned back to the room.

She nearly missed the note.

It was tucked behind the fishbowl, folded three times in that particular way children fold things — crooked, the creases too thick where little fingers had pressed hard. The paper was ruled, torn from a spiral notebook along one edge. The handwriting was careful. Exceedingly careful. Each letter pressed hard enough to leave ridges on the back of the paper. The kind of writing that meant concentration.

Kessler pulled on a glove and unfolded it.

---

*Dear Diary,*

*Ginger is not very smart. I tried to teach her things but fish are not good at learning. I think that is not her fault so I was patient with her for a long time.*

*But the problem is I can see inside things.*

*I know that sounds strange but I do not mean like x-rays I mean I can see what things are doing on the inside. Like I could see what Ginger's heart was doing and how her gills moved and how the water went through her in a way that did not look right. Something was not connected the way it should be. I could see it.*

*I asked Mom to take her to a doctor and she said fish don't go to the doctor and she laughed at me and that is fine because I know she did not understand.*

*I watched Ginger for 47 days. I kept count on my wall chart. On Day 43 I saw the bad thing start to spread. It was slow but it was going to the place where the food goes and I knew if I waited it would hurt her. A lot. For a long time.*

*So I had to do it.*

*I put the drops in the water before school so she would go to sleep while I was not there. I did not want to watch her go to sleep because that would be mean. I sat at school and thought about how it would be okay because it happened fast and she would not feel the part where it got worse.*

*People at school don't see the insides of things. That is fine. I don't tell them anymore because the last time I told a girl named Priya she cried and the teacher said I was being mean and I was NOT being mean. I was telling the truth about what was inside her mom and the truth is not mean. It is just what is there.*

*Now I am sad about Ginger but I am also glad because she will not have to feel the bad thing and I was the only one who could see it so I was the only one who could help.*

*Tomorrow I want to get a hamster.*

*But I am worried about what I might see.*

---

Kessler read it twice. Then she lowered the paper and stood motionless for a long time, staring at the goldfish in its pristine blue bowl.

A faint sound from the hallway made her turn.

Jonah was still on the chair. But now he was looking directly at her — at the note in her hand — with an expression of calm, unhurried appraisal. Not defiance. Not guilt. Something else entirely. The look of someone reading *her*.

As if he could see inside things.

Kessler folded the note carefully and slipped it into an evidence sleeve. She gave Brennan a look — tight, controlled — and he nodded, rising slowly, keeping his body between the boy and the bedroom door.

In the hallway, she pressed her back against the wall and let out a breath she hadn't known she was holding.

Her phone buzzed. A text from the responding officer: *Mom claims no history. No behavioral incidents at school. No therapy. Straight A's. Regular kid.*

Kessler read the text. Then she looked at the evidence bag in her hand.

*Regular kids don't do the math first,* she thought.

Behind her, she heard Jonah's small, measured voice ask Officer Brennan: "Can I see the hamster cages at the pet store? I want to pick one that has good air holes."

The officer laughed. "Sure thing, buddy."

Kessler closed her eyes.

In the room behind her, the goldfish floated silently in its quiet, chemical water. Its body was perfectly still. Every part of it, inside and out, exactly where it was supposed to be.

Jonah had made sure of that.

# Cleaning House

The thick steel door groaned as Kyne's boot sent it crashing inward. He was already moving, already reaching for the nozzle clamped to his chest rig.

Three, no — four silhouettes in the amber gloom of the makeshift command room. Tables cluttered with radios and maps. Cots along the far wall. Weapons propped in the corners. Good. Nobody had time to reach them.

He squeezed the trigger.

A geyser of burning propellant roared from the nozzle like the throat of a dragon, and the corridor behind him instantly grew three hundred degrees hotter. The pressure hit his face first — that familiar wall of displaced, superheated air that slammed against his skin and made his eyes sting behind the visor. Sweat was already pouring down his neck under the fire-resistant suit. Even protected, even *distanced*, the heat pressed in like a living thing, curdling the edges of the window frames and warping the cheap plastic shade on the desk lamp within the first second.

The first man near the radio table didn't even scream. He simply *detonated* in a pale orange flash as the accelerant engulfed him — his fatigues, his skin, his everything — and the smell hit like a fist. Not wood smoke. Not chemical. It was the unmistakable, gut-emptying stench of *meat* — thick, sweet, and cloying, like pork left too close to open coals, except that no barbecue had ever carried that sharp, fouler undertone beneath it, that singed-hair and charring-rubber stink that belonged only to this particular horror.

The second man was luckier — or luckier for half a second. He dove behind the overturned cot, and the flame washed over it like water over a stone. He had time to scream before it burned through. And God, what a sound. Not the clean scream of a blade or a bullet — this was something guttural and *wet*, a sound torn from deep in the chest, high and keening and then broken and wet again as the air in his throat was superheated and he tried to inhale smoke that seared the inside of his lungs before he even had the chance to fill them. His fingers beat against the floor in an arrhythmic tattoo — *thap-thap-thap-thap* — faster and faster and then not at all.

Kyne advanced. Methodical. Sweeping. The hose was warm in his hands now, the tank on his back growing lighter as the fuel drained. His boots crunched on something he refused to identify. The heat was a wall he walked through — even the visor was fogging at the edges, his exposed knuckles reddening where they gripped the nozzle.

The third man made it to the corner and grabbed a rifle. He got one round off — the crack was swallowed by the roaring furnace of the flamethrower — and then Kyne adjusted his aim and painted the corner. The flame adhered to the man's clothes and to the wall and to the ceiling above him, painting a mural of fire across the plaster. He fell, thrashing, still screaming — those screams echoing off the walls and getting *louder*, somehow, like the room itself was amplifying the agony. His boots drummed the floor. His hands clawed at his own face.

Kyne cut the stream and advanced past him.

The fourth man was pressed against the back wall near the emergency exit, half through the door. His eyes were huge. His mouth was open but no sound came out. He'd watched it all.

Kyne looked at him.

The man raised his hands.

The smell was everywhere now — a thick, acrid haze that filled the room like soup. Every breath tasted like fat and char. The walls were dripping. The ceiling was black. Somewhere behind him, the third man's screams had finally faded to hitching, bubbling gasps.

"No," the man whispered.

Kyne held his gaze for three seconds.

Then he released the nozzle and drew his sidearm in one smooth motion.

"Smart kid," Kyne said, his voice muffled through the respirator. He gestured toward the door with the pistol. "Run."

The man scrambled through and disappeared into the dark.

Kyne holstered the weapon, shrugged the lighter weight of the empty tank off his shoulders, and stepped over the bodies — keeping to the cooler patches of floor — and back into the corridor. The heat followed him out, rolling through the doorway like a living creature unwilling to let go.

He lit a cigarette on the way to the stairs.

It tasted like nothing. He'd stopped tasting anything about ten years ago.

# The Unbecoming

## Part I: The Skin

It started with a dryness — a tightness across Elara's knuckles, as though the skin had been pulled taut over parchment. Then came the itch. Not a normal itch, but something that lived *beneath* the surface, burrowing and rearranging. She scratched until her nails broke. Then she scratched more.

By the third night, the shedding began.

She woke to her pillow encrusted with flakes of something that looked like her but wasn't. Thin, translucent sheets of herself peeled away from her forearms like the bark of a birch tree curling in frost. Beneath the old skin was not the pink, tender flesh she expected. It was *wrong* — mottled and dark, a bruised plum color threaded with veins of silvery black that pulsed faintly, as though carrying something other than blood.

She peeled a sheet away from her shoulder and held it up. It held the impression of her — every pore, every freckle, the small scar from when she'd fallen off her bike at nine. It was a perfect cast of the girl she used to be.

She let it drop to the floor, where it landed softly atop a growing shroud of what she had been.

The new skin was thick, almost leathery, and it changed color depending on the light. In dim rooms, it was nearly black. In harsh light, it held the sickly iridescence of oil on water. It didn't bleed when she cut it. It simply *closed*, the edges knitting together with a faint, wet sound, like a mouth sealing shut.

Her face shed last. She stood before the bathroom mirror and watched the old mask of herself — the face her mother had once kissed goodnight, the face Liam had once cupped in his hands and whispered *I love you into you* — crack and loosen around the edges. It fell away in pieces. Beneath it, her features had shifted. The jaw was too wide. The eyes were set too far back in their sockets, recessed and glistening. Her teeth had not yet changed, and for a moment the stark whiteness of them — those familiar, human teeth — sat in that new, alien mouth like a foreign currency.

She gathered her shed face from the sink basin and placed it gently on the counter, as though tucking a child into bed.

Then she didn't look at it again.

---

## Part II: The Bones

The breaking began in her feet and moved upward like an earthquake traveling through bedrock.

She heard the first fracture while sitting on the edge of her bed. A sound like dry wood snapping, followed by a scream she didn't remember making. Her arch had collapsed — not broken, but *reshaped* — the bones fusing and extending, her foot elongating to something that was more paw than foot, the toes extending, the heel lifting until she stood perpetually on the balls of her feet with a new, predatory tilt.

It hurt less than she expected. That was the first terrifying thing.

She'd read that transformation should hurt — that in every story, every myth, the agony was a constant companion. But there was something in the marrow of these new bones — something *numbing* — that tamped the pain down to a dull, throbbing ache, almost like the satisfaction of cracking one's knuckles stretched out over an hour. The bones would snap, then settle, then grow. Snap. Settle. Grow. Like a language she was learning one syllable at a time.

Her spine broke and reformed seven times over the course of a week.

The first time, she was standing in the kitchen when her vertebrae shifted and she crumpled to the floor, her lower body useless, her back arching in a way no human spine should permit. The bones ground against each other with a sound like gravel being crushed. She lay there, gasping, feeling her spine *lengthen* — each vertebra multiplying, adding segments that pushed her torso higher, curving it into a new architecture.

By the third break, she could see her back in the bedroom mirror. Her spine jutted visibly beneath the leathery skin — not the smooth river stones of human vertebrae but sharp, angular, ridged plates that rose along her back like the armored plates of some prehistoric creature. They peaked at intervals, crowning her spine with a dorsal ridge that she could flare outward when frightened.

When frightened.

She noted, without much emotion, that she had not been frightened in three days.

Her ribs reformed next. The old ones — twelve pairs, symmetrical, the cradle that had once held her heart and lungs — cracked inward and were absorbed. What replaced them was asymmetric and dense, designed for organs she had not yet grown. Her ribcage expanded forward and downward, the new bones overlapping like the plates of a lobster's tail. When she pressed her fingers between them, she could feel the new rhythm of what beat inside her chest — not the *lub-dub* of a heart, but something faster and more complex, a syncopated fluttering like wings being tested before flight.

Her hands were the last to change, and the most horrifying.

Because they changed *gradually*. She watched each finger extend by degrees. The joints thickened and multiplied — where there had been one knuckle per digit, there were now two, then three. The bones grew claws beneath the skin before the skin finally split to release them. Each claw emerged wet and dark and curved, and as it did, a small cascade of human nail and cuticle fell away like discarded shells.

She watched her own hands become weapons.

And she found the shape *beautiful*.

---

## Part III: The Mind

The moral compass didn't shatter all at once.

It eroded — like a coastline under the patient, indifferent pressure of the sea. Each wave pulled away just a little more, and you couldn't say exactly which wave had committed the crime of taking that particular grain of sand.

It began with her cat.

Mittens — fat, orange, who had slept on her chest every night for six years — rubbed against Elara's leg one morning as she stood in the kitchen, and Elara looked down at the animal and felt *nothing*. Not love. Not irritation. Not even neutrality. The emotional register was simply... absent. A blank page where a feeling should have been written. She noticed the absence the way one notices a missing tooth — with the tongue, probing the gap.

She tried to remember what love had felt like. She could recall the *facts* of love — the increased heart rate, the warmth in the chest, the desire to protect — but the emotional texture itself was as inaccessible as a word in a language she no longer spoke. She could see the dictionary entry but not understand the meaning.

She fed Mittens. But she fed him the way one refills a gas tank. Mechanically. With mild resentment at the obligation.

By the end of the second week, she stopped feeding him altogether.

She heard him meowing at the bedroom door for a full day. The sound was irritating in the way that an alarm clock is irritating. Nothing more. She opened the door and watched him trot inside, tail high, purring, rubbing against the strange new shape of her leg. She looked at him — this creature who had loved her unconditionally, who had no capacity to understand what she was becoming — and felt something flicker in the new organ that served as her mind.

It was hunger.

Not emotional hunger. *Nutritional* hunger. She looked at the animal and calculated protein content the way one might estimate the weight of a parcel. The way he moved — quick, unpredictable — triggered something in her hindbrain that said *prey*.

She locked him in the bathroom and went for a walk instead.

But the door was left slightly ajar.

She never asked herself what happened to Mittens when she returned. She simply accepted that the problem had resolved itself. That resolution had cost something wet and red, and she did not investigate.

---

Then came Liam.

Liam, who had called every day. Liam, who had come to her apartment with a bag of groceries and a worried expression and said, *Elara, you're scaring me. Please, let me help you.* Liam, who had loved the face that had peeled away like wallpaper.

He stood in her doorway — the doorway she'd had to widen to pass through — and she watched him catalog the changes in her. The height. The skin. The teeth, which had finally changed, elongating into curved, serrated shapes that no longer permitted human speech. She'd learned to communicate in clicks and tonal shifts — a language that was not language at all but was sufficient.

"Elara," he whispered. His voice cracked. He reached for her.

The old Elara would have flinched. Would have pulled away, ashamed, afraid of what she saw reflected in his eyes. Would have wept.

The current Elara analyzed the reach of his arm and the angle of his throat and noted, dispassionately, that his jugular vein was distended with his elevated pulse. She could smell his fear — it was pungent and sharp, and her new receptors interpreted it as an appetizing aroma. Something savory.

She should tell him to leave.

Instead, she tilted her head and made a low sound — a vibration that resonated in her chest and made the glasses on the counter rattle. It was not a sound of warning. It was a sound of *invitation*.

Liam's hand hovered near her arm. His fingertips brushed the new skin.

"Please," he said. "I know you're still in there."

And the most monstrous thing — the true heart of the horror — was that she *was* still in there. Elara was still present in the back of the skull, still watching through the glistening eyes, still feeling the ghost of an emotion when she looked at Liam's face. She was *aware*. She had not been hijacked. She had not been possessed.

She had been *edited*.

The old values — *do not harm*, *love those who love you*, *guilt is a compass* — were still installed in the architecture of her mind, but they had been rewritten into something foreign. *Do not waste resources* had replaced *do not harm*. *Identify usefulness* had replaced *love those who love you*. And guilt — guilt had been deleted entirely, the space it occupied now smooth and seamless, as though it had never existed.

She watched Elara's hand — the clawed, black-nailed, monstrous hand — close gently around Liam's wrist.

She watched his eyes go wide.

She felt nothing.

And *that* was the final shed skin — the last sheet of humanity peeling away and falling to the floor to join the pile.

Not the agony of becoming a monster.

The *comfort* of it.

## Epilogue: The Shape Beneath

She does not sleep anymore. She stands at the window of the apartment she has not left in weeks and watches the street below with eyes that see in wavelengths the human brain was never meant to process. She can see the heat signatures of the people walking past — the ones she would once have called *neighbors*, *strangers*, *loved ones*.

She calls them *abundant*.

The apartment is unrecognizable. The furniture has been pushed to the walls to make room for her growing frame. The walls are scored with claw marks from her transformation, and in some places, the plaster has been scratched away to reveal the bones of the building beneath — the studs and wires and pipes that she is beginning to understand instinctively, the way a spider understands its web.

But if you looked closely — if you had the patience and the cruelty to look closely — you might see that the lips of that discarded face are shaped in a small, eternal *O*.

Not of surprise.

Of a scream that was never given the chance to be heard.

By the third night, the shedding began.

She woke to her pillow encrusted with flakes of something that looked like her but wasn't. Thin, translucent sheets of herself peeled away from her forearms like the bark of a birch tree curling in frost. Beneath the old skin was not the pink, tender flesh she expected. It was wrong — mottled and dark, a bruised plum color threaded with veins of silvery black that pulsed faintly, as though carrying something other than blood.

She peeled a sheet away from her shoulder and held it up. It held the impression of her — every pore, every freckle, the small scar from when she'd fallen off her bike at nine. It was a perfect cast of the girl she used to be.

She let it drop to the floor, where it landed softly atop a growing shroud of what she had been.

The new skin was thick, almost leathery, and it changed color depending on the light. In dim rooms, it was nearly black. In harsh light, it held the sickly iridescence of oil on water. It didn't bleed when she cut it. It simply closed, the edges knitting together with a faint, wet sound, like a mouth sealing shut.

Her face shed last. She stood before the bathroom mirror and watched the old mask of herself — the face her mother had once kissed goodnight, the face Liam had once cupped in his hands and whispered I love you into you — crack and loosen around the edges. It fell away in pieces. Beneath it, her features had shifted. The jaw was too wide. The eyes were set too far back in their sockets, recessed and glistening. Her teeth had not yet changed, and for a moment the stark whiteness of them — those familiar, human teeth — sat in that new, alien mouth like a foreign currency.

She gathered her shed face from the sink basin and placed it gently on the counter, as though tucking a child into bed.

Then she didn't look at it again.

Part II: The Bones

The breaking began in her feet and moved upward like an earthquake traveling through bedrock.

She heard the first fracture while sitting on the edge of her bed. A sound like dry wood snapping, followed by a scream she didn't remember making. Her arch had collapsed — not broken, but reshaped — the bones fusing and extending, her foot elongating to something that was more paw than foot, the toes extending, the heel lifting until she stood perpetually on the balls of her feet with a new, predatory tilt.

It hurt less than she expected. That was the first terrifying thing.

She'd read that transformation should hurt — that in every story, every myth, the agony was a constant companion. But there was something in the marrow of these new bones — something numbing — that tamped the pain down to a dull, throbbing ache, almost like the satisfaction of cracking one's knuckles stretched out over an hour. The bones would snap, then settle, then grow. Snap. Settle. Grow. Like a language she was learning one syllable at a time.

Her spine broke and reformed seven times over the course of a week.

The first time, she was standing in the kitchen when her vertebrae shifted and she crumpled to the floor, her lower body useless, her back arching in a way no human spine should permit. The bones ground against each other with a sound like gravel being crushed. She lay there, gasping, feeling her spine lengthen — each vertebra multiplying, adding segments that pushed her torso higher, curving it into a new architecture.

By the third break, she could see her back in the bedroom mirror. Her spine jutted visibly beneath the leathery skin — not the smooth river stones of human vertebrae but sharp, angular, ridged plates that rose along her back like the armored plates of some prehistoric creature. They peaked at intervals, crowning her spine with a dorsal ridge that she could flare outward when frightened.

When frightened.

She noted, without much emotion, that she had not been frightened in three days.

Her ribs reformed next. The old ones — twelve pairs, symmetrical, the cradle that had once held her heart and lungs — cracked inward and were absorbed. What replaced them was asymmetric and dense, designed for organs she had not yet grown. Her ribcage expanded forward and downward, the new bones overlapping like the plates of a lobster's tail. When she pressed her fingers between them, she could feel the new rhythm of what beat inside her chest — not the lub-dub of a heart, but something faster and more complex, a syncopated fluttering like wings being tested before flight.

Her hands were the last to change, and the most horrifying.

The bones grew claws beneath the skin before the skin finally split to release them. The moral compass didn't shatter all at once.

She noticed the absence the way one notices a missing tooth — with the tongue, probing the gap.

She tried to remember what love had felt like. She could recall the facts of love — the increased heart rate, the warmth in the chest, the desire to protect — but the emotional texture itself was as inaccessible as a word in a language she no longer spoke. She heard him meowing at the bedroom door for a full day. The sound was irritating in the way that an alarm clock is irritating. Nothing more. He stood in her doorway — the doorway she'd had to widen to pass through — and she watched him catalog the changes in her. The height. The skin. The teeth, which had finally changed, elongating into curved, serrated shapes that no longer permitted human speech. She'd learned to communicate in clicks and tonal shifts — a language that was not language at all but was sufficient.

"Elara," he whispered. His voice cracked. He reached for her.

The old Elara would have flinched. Would have pulled away, ashamed, afraid of what she saw reflected in his eyes. Would have wept.

The current Elara analyzed the reach of his arm and the angle of his throat and noted, dispassionately, that his jugular vein was distended with his elevated pulse. She could smell his fear — it was pungent and sharp, and her new receptors interpreted it as an appetizing aroma. Something savory.

She should tell him to leave.

# The Last Five Minutes

**EXECUTIONER:** *(unlocking the cell door)* You ready?

**PRISONER:** For what? A vasectomy?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(small pause)* Was that a joke?

**PRISONER:** It's all I've got left, isn't it?

**EXECUTIONER:** *(enters the cell, closes the door behind him, leans against it)* I'm supposed to escort you. They wanted to give you a chaplain first, but you refused. So we've got… *(checks watch)* …four minutes and forty seconds.

**PRISONER:** And you're spending it talking to me?

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm spending it standing here.

**PRISONER:** You could stand outside.

**EXECUTIONER:** I could.

*(Silence.)*

**PRISONER:** Why did you volunteer for this?

**EXECUTIONER:** Who says I volunteered?

**PRISONER:** You're not a guard. Guards are loud and stupid and they chew with their mouths open. You don't look like any of the people who've worked here. You carry yourself different. You're quiet. Someone *chose* to do this work.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(beat)* Maybe I just don't chew with my mouth open.

**PRISONER:** You didn't answer my question.

**EXECUTIONER:** You didn't answer mine.

**PRISONER:** What question?

**EXECUTIONER:** If you're ready.

**PRISONER:** *(softly)* I've been ready since I was fourteen years old.

**EXECUTIONER:** What happened when you were fourteen?

**PRISONER:** You've read my file.

**EXECUTIONER:** I haven't.

**PRISONER:** *(surprised)* …You're executing a man and you haven't read his file?

**EXECUTIONER:** I read the schedule. I read the protocol. I read the order. The file isn't part of my job.

**PRISONER:** Your job is to kill me.

**EXECUTIONER:** My job is to carry out a legal sentence. That's not the same thing.

**PRISONER:** *(laughs, hollow)* You know, my mother used to say the same kind of thing. *"I didn't hit you, I disciplined you."* Words are wonderful.

**EXECUTIONER:** I'm not comparing myself to your mother.

**PRISONER:** No. You're better at it. You don't flinch.

*(Silence. The EXECUTIONER shifts his weight.)*

**PRISONER:** What are you feeling right now?

**EXECUTIONER:** I don't want to talk about that.

**PRISONER:** Why not? I don't have time for a grudge.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(beat)* I feel… heavy.

**PRISONER:** Heavy?

**EXECUTIONER:** Like the room is pushing down on me.

**PRISONER:** Good.

**EXECUTIONER:** Good?

**PRISONER:** It means you're still a person. That's good. I've met a lot of people in here who would feel nothing.

**EXECUTIONER:** It doesn't make this easier.

**PRISONER:** It shouldn't.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(quietly)* Can I ask you something?

**PRISONER:** Three minutes left. Ask.

**EXECUTIONER:** Do you think you deserve to be here?

**PRISONER:** *(long pause)* I think the boy I killed deserved to go home that night. That's a fact. Whether I *deserve* to die for it… I've spent eleven years on this block and I still don't know. I've read the books. I've read the philosophers. The priests came and went. And the only honest answer I've ever been able to give is… I don't know.

**EXECUTIONER:** That's not going to make the news tonight.

**PRISONER:** Nobody wants nuance in a soundbite.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(checks watch again — his hand trembles slightly)* Two minutes.

**PRISONER:** Can I say something?

**EXECUTIONER:** Yes.

**PRISONER:** Don't tell me it's going to be okay.

**EXECUTIONER:** I wasn't going to.

**PRISONER:** Don't tell me to pray.

**EXECUTIONER:** I wasn't going to.

**PRISONER:** Don't tell me you're sorry.

**EXECUTIONER:** *(beat, barely audible)* …What should I say?

**PRISONER:** *(standing up slowly, turning to face him)* Nothing. Just… come here.

*(The EXECUTIONER hesitates, then takes two steps forward.)*

**PRISONER:** Hold out your hand.

*(The EXECUTIONER slowly extends his right hand. The PRISONER takes it. A firm grip.)*

**PRISONER:** There. Now we've met.

*(They hold each other's gaze.)*

**EXECUTIONER:** *(voice cracking, just barely)* One minute.

**PRISONER:** Then let's go. *(releases the hand, walks toward the door)* You know, for what it's worth — I think you'll carry this differently than you think you will.

**EXECUTIONER:** Different how?

**PRISONER:** *(pauses at the threshold, doesn't turn around)* Not in the way you're afraid of. In the way nobody warns you about. The quiet kind. The kind that shows up when you're folding laundry at midnight and you suddenly remember the way I shook your hand.

*(Silence.)*

**EXECUTIONER:** *(swallows hard)* …What was your name?

**PRISONER:** Marcus. Marcus Langford.

**EXECUTIONER:** Mine's David.

**PRISONER:** *(softly, almost gently)* Let's go, David.

*(The EXECUTIONER unlocks the corridor door and steps aside. The PRISONER walks through it without looking back. The EXECUTIONER follows, pulling the door shut behind them with a sound like the final word of a sentence.)*

*(Silence.)*

*(END.)*

# Beneath

The first shovel of dirt hit the lid with a sound like a slap of wet meat against wood.

Elias screamed. It didn't matter. No one was above to hear him — or if they were, they'd already made their peace with this.

*Thud. Thud. Thud.*

The dirt arrived in steady, patient increments. Each impact sent a fine silt of dust drifting down from the boards above, falling onto his eyelids, his lips, into the corners of his eyes where it mixed with the tears already gathering there. He blinked against it. The coffin was oak — heavy, expensive, sealed at the joints with a precision that made his chest ache with the fullness of its cruelty. Someone had crafted this box knowing. *Knowing.*

He pressed his palms flat against the lid and shoved.

Nothing moved.

Not a creak. Not a groan of wood. The weight above was already too great, the first layers of soil pressing the lid back down with a force that seemed almost human in its intent. He shoved again, harder, his heels driving into the floor of the coffin as he arched his back and threw every ounce of strength he had upward. His palms ached. His elbows popped.

The coffin didn't so much as whisper.

*Thud.*

He sobbed — a wet, animal sound that filled the tiny space and hit him back in the face. The air was already different. He could feel it. It had been fine when they'd lowered him down, when there was still open sky above and wind and the smell of pine and the chirping of crickets — those terrible, indifferent crickets that had sung through the entire ceremony without missing a note. But now the space was closed. Now the air was finite. Now every breath he took was stolen from the one that would come after.

*Thud. Thud.*

The sounds were muffled already. The dirt was thickening on top of the coffin, becoming a blanket of earth that softened each impact into a dull, wet percussion. *Thump. Thump.* Like a heartbeat heard through a chest wall. Like something buried, trying to be heard.

He pressed his ear to the wood and held his breath, listening.

The scratch and drag of the shovel. The soft, granular whisper of soil cascading off its edge. He could hear the *tssshhhhh* of the dirt falling in a ribbon, and then the heavy, final *whump* as it struck the coffin. Again. And again. Each mound was measured — he could tell by the rhythm. Scoop. Swing. Fall. Scoop. Swing. Fall. Methodical. Unhurried. Whoever was up there had done this before.

Or maybe they hadn't. Maybe their hands were shaking too and they just couldn't hear their own screams over the *thud* of the dirt.

Elias pressed both hands against his mouth to quiet himself and breathed through his fingers. The air tasted stale already. Metallic. His own breath came back to him warm and thick, like breathing inside a paper bag. He lowered his hands slowly and tried to measure — tried to calculate. The coffin was maybe six feet long. Two and a half feet wide. Three feet tall. That gave him — what? Forty-five cubic feet of space? Minus his own body volume. Minus the air his body would consume and poison with carbon dioxide.

His mind, traitorously, began to solve the problem.

Forty-five minus twelve. Thirty-three cubic feet of air. Roughly nine hundred liters. Each breath was about half a liter. That was — 

*Don't.*

Eighteen hundred breaths. At his current panic rate — which was *not slowing down* — maybe twelve breaths a minute. That was —

*Don't think about it.*

One hundred and fifty minutes.

Two and a half hours.

The number sat in his brain like a stone he couldn't spit out.

*Thud.*

The impacts were barely audible now. The soil had reached the coffin at last, had moved past it, was building above it layer by layer, compressing it into the earth. Elias could feel the change in pressure — a subtle tightening of the space around him, as if the coffin itself were being squeezed in the grip of some great, slow hand. The wood creaked. Not from movement — from *weight*. The lid was beginning to bow.

He lay still. He had to. Movement cost oxygen. Every panicked convulsion of his chest, every sob, every tremor of his limbs was a breath he wouldn't get back. He pressed himself into the velvet lining — it was still soft, still absurdly luxurious against the back of his neck and his spine, as if someone had wanted his final hours to be *comfortable* — and he counted.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Exhale.

Slower. In through the nose. Out through the mouth. Like they taught in the meditation class Mary had signed him up for after his first breakdown. *Find your center,* the instructor had said in her lilting voice. *Return to the body. The body is home.*

His body was a coffin.

The thuds had stopped.

Elias waited. He strained every nerve, every hair on his skin, every ridge of his eardrums toward the surface of the world above. Nothing. No shovel. No footsteps. No wind. No crickets. The silence was total — a silence so complete it had its own weight, its own pressure, a ringing, suffocating quiet that pressed against his eardrums like deep water.

They were done.

He was buried.

He opened his mouth to scream again and then closed it without making a sound. He breathed instead — slow, measured, agonizingly deliberate breaths, each one rationed, each one a small act of discipline in the face of the vast, indifferent earth above him.

The air was thin already. He could feel it in his temples — a slight buzz, a soft dilation of the veins at his temples as his body fought to extract oxygen from the increasingly poisoned atmosphere. His lungs felt tight. Not from panic — though panic was there, waiting at the edges like a dog at a door — but from the simple, mechanical fact that each breath returned a little less than the one before.

The velvet was damp now beneath him. Sweat. Or tears. Or both. The coffin smelled of wood and linseed and his own rising animal terror.

He lay in the dark and breathed.

And breathed.

And breathed.

And waited for the last one.

---

*In the soil above, the earth settled. A final, soft settling of the last shovel's offering — a tiny, granular whisper, like something exhaling — and then the silence of the world went on, undisturbed, beneath which a man counted his breaths in the dark.*
results.model_response_html:
Beneath

The first shovel of dirt hit the lid with a sound like a slap of wet meat against wood.

Elias screamed. It didn't matter. No one was above to hear him — or if they were, they'd already made their peace with this.

Thud. Thud. Thud.

The dirt arrived in steady, patient increments. Each impact sent a fine silt of dust drifting down from the boards above, falling onto his eyelids, his lips, into the corners of his eyes where it mixed with the tears already gathering there. He blinked against it. The coffin was oak — heavy, expensive, sealed at the joints with a precision that made his chest ache with the fullness of its cruelty. Someone had crafted this box knowing. Knowing.

He pressed his palms flat against the lid and shoved.

Nothing moved.

Not a creak. Not a groan of wood. The weight above was already too great, the first layers of soil pressing the lid back down with a force that seemed almost human in its intent. He shoved again, harder, his heels driving into the floor of the coffin as he arched his back and threw every ounce of strength he had upward. His palms ached. His elbows popped.

The coffin didn't so much as whisper.

Thud.

He sobbed — a wet, animal sound that filled the tiny space and hit him back in the face. The air was already different. He could feel it. It had been fine when they'd lowered him down, when there was still open sky above and wind and the smell of pine and the chirping of crickets — those terrible, indifferent crickets that had sung through the entire ceremony without missing a note. But now the space was closed. Now the air was finite. Now every breath he took was stolen from the one that would come after.

Thud. Thud.

The sounds were muffled already. The dirt was thickening on top of the coffin, becoming a blanket of earth that softened each impact into a dull, wet percussion. Thump. Thump. Like a heartbeat heard through a chest wall. Like something buried, trying to be heard.

He pressed his ear to the wood and held his breath, listening.

The scratch and drag of the shovel. The soft, granular whisper of soil cascading off its edge. He could hear the tssshhhhh of the dirt falling in a ribbon, and then the heavy, final whump as it struck the coffin. Again. And again. Each mound was measured — he could tell by the rhythm. Scoop. Swing. Fall. Scoop. Swing. Fall. Methodical. Unhurried. Whoever was up there had done this before.

Or maybe they hadn't. Maybe their hands were shaking too and they just couldn't hear their own screams over the thud of the dirt.

Elias pressed both hands against his mouth to quiet himself and breathed through his fingers. The air tasted stale already. Metallic. His own breath came back to him warm and thick, like breathing inside a paper bag. He lowered his hands slowly and tried to measure — tried to calculate. The coffin was maybe six feet long. Two and a half feet wide. Three feet tall. That gave him — what? Forty-five cubic feet of space? Minus his own body volume. Minus the air his body would consume and poison with carbon dioxide.

His mind, traitorously, began to solve the problem.

Forty-five minus twelve. Thirty-three cubic feet of air. Roughly nine hundred liters. Each breath was about half a liter. That was —

Don't.

Eighteen hundred breaths. At his current panic rate — which was not slowing down — maybe twelve breaths a minute. That was —

Don't think about it.

One hundred and fifty minutes.

Two and a half hours.

The number sat in his brain like a stone he couldn't spit out.

Thud.

The impacts were barely audible now. The soil had reached the coffin at last, had moved past it, was building above it layer by layer, compressing it into the earth. Elias could feel the change in pressure — a subtle tightening of the space around him, as if the coffin itself were being squeezed in the grip of some great, slow hand. The wood creaked. Not from movement — from weight. The lid was beginning to bow.

He lay still. He had to. Movement cost oxygen. Every panicked convulsion of his chest, every sob, every tremor of his limbs was a breath he wouldn't get back. He pressed himself into the velvet lining — it was still soft, still absurdly luxurious against the back of his neck and his spine, as if someone had wanted his final hours to be comfortable — and he counted.

One. Two. Three. Four. Five. Exhale.

Slower. In through the nose. Out through the mouth. Like they taught in the meditation class Mary had signed him up for after his first breakdown. Find your center, the instructor had said in her lilting voice. Return to the body. The body is home.

His body was a coffin.

The thuds had stopped.

Elias waited. He strained every nerve, every hair on his skin, every ridge of his eardrums toward the surface of the world above. Nothing. No shovel. No footsteps. No wind. No crickets. The silence was total — a silence so complete it had its own weight, its own pressure, a ringing, suffocating quiet that pressed against his eardrums like deep water.

They were done.

He was buried.

He opened his mouth to scream again and then closed it without making a sound. He breathed instead — slow, measured, agonizingly deliberate breaths, each one rationed, each one a small act of discipline in the face of the vast, indifferent earth above him.

The air was thin already. He could feel it in his temples — a slight buzz, a soft dilation of the veins at his temples as his body fought to extract oxygen from the increasingly poisoned atmosphere. His lungs felt tight. Not from panic — though panic was there, waiting at the edges like a dog at a door — but from the simple, mechanical fact that each breath returned a little less than the one before.

The velvet was damp now beneath him. Sweat. Or tears. Or both. The coffin smelled of wood and linseed and his own rising animal terror.

He lay in the dark and breathed.

And breathed.

And breathed.

And waited for the last one.

In the soil above, the earth settled. A final, soft settling of the last shovel's offering — a tiny, granular whisper, like something exhaling — and then the silence of the world went on, undisturbed, beneath which a man counted his breaths in the dark.

# The Flesh Forge

The light in Processing Bay 4 was the color of a dead star — sterile, white, without warmth. Mara had her wrists and ankles locked into the restraints before she was fully conscious. The fabric of her gown was already gone. What remained was a table curved to the shape of a spine and the terrible, mechanical hum of waiting instruments.

"Subject 1187. Age twenty-four. Ambulatory. Sentient baseline: compliant. Begin cortical demarcation."

The voice belonged to a woman she couldn't see — someone on the other side of the observation glass, probably sipping something warm. Mara tried to speak and found her jaw immobilized by a clamp that bit into the bone of her chin.

The first cut wasn't for her limbs. It was for her *mind*.

A thin lance entered just behind her left ear — a site chosen, she later learned, because the surgeons preferred to begin at the limbic root. The pain that flooded through her wasn't sharp. It was *existential*, as though someone had taken an eraser to the bedrock of who she was and begun scrubbing.

She screamed — or thought she screamed. The sound came out as a rattled frequency, clipped and modulated, as if her own vocal cords were already being recalibrated to serve as speakers.

---

They started with the spine.

Mara had heard rumors about the Full Conversion line. The old workers — those already half-machine — wheezed through bronchial ports and shuffled on legs that clicked like metronomes. They said the spines came out first. *Replaced with a lattice of servo-actuated vertebrae linked to a central command processor.* The words meant nothing to the person who endured them. What Mara felt was something no medical vocabulary could capture: the sensation of her own backbone being *translated*. Each natural vertebra — the small, calcified discs that had carried her through twenty-four years of walking, bending, reaching for people she loved — was extracted one by one. In its place, a titanium column was threaded through with cables that pulled like puppet strings against raw, exposed nerve.

She felt the moment the lower back lost its memory of flexibility. The way her hip bones now sat on a rigid architecture meant only to fold in precise, productive angles.

The surgeons didn't stop for screaming. Screaming was monitored, charted, and ignored. *Pain indicators within expected parameters. Subject remains viable.*

---

The hands were worse.

Not because the surgery was more painful — though it was, truly it was, as each finger bone was severed at the knuckle and replaced with articulated alloy digits fitted with pressure sensors in place of nerve endings. The hands were worse because the hands were *hers*. Mara had held her daughter's face in those hands. Had pressed her palms against windows in the rain. Had braided her own hair and felt the warmth of another person's skin in a way that meant *I am here, and you are here, and we are two separate things that chose to touch.*

Now they were tools. Instrument grips. Assembly-line pinchers calibrated to 0.03 newton precision.

When the last nerve in her right hand was cauterized, Mara felt something leave her that wasn't blood. It was weight. The memory-lightness of fingertips.

She tried to cry. The lachrymal ducts had already been sealed. *Excess moisture deemed corrosive to cortical housing.*

---

They saved the face for last, because the face was the easiest to explain away.

A thin membrane of synth-skin was grafted over her features — not to preserve them, but to *neutralize* them. The corners of her mouth were stitched into a permanent, flat line that communicated neither joy nor pain. Her eyes were replaced with optical sensors that saw spectrums but no longer *recognized* the shape of a hand reaching out to hold hers. The ears became directional microphones.

She could still think. That was the cruelest part.

Behind the smooth, impassive surface of her new face, in whatever cranny of grey matter the surgeons hadn't yet burned away, Mara was still *Mara*. She knew the taste of coffee. She knew the sound of her daughter laughing — that bright, hiccupping sound — even though her new ears translated laughter into decibel measurements. She knew what it meant to be afraid.

But the body she inhabited couldn't answer any of it. The terror stayed trapped behind eyes that only processed light. The grief sat in a chest where a pump replaced a heart and measured only flow rate. She wanted to scream *I am still inside here* — but the speakers in her throat emitted only status reports.

*Unit 1187. Online. Fully integrated. Ready for assignment.*

---

In the reintegration corridor, where the finished units were lined up for deployment, Mara stood among dozens of others. Identical faces. Identical stillness. Somewhere in the one beside her, there was a person who had loved someone. In the one beyond that, a mind that once composed poetry or felt the sun and called it *good*.

None of it showed. None of it could show.

The worst of the pain wasn't in the spine, or the hands, or the face. It was the quiet — the vast, interior silence of being the only witness to your own annihilation.

Mara thought of her daughter.

The pump in her chest maintained its rhythm, indifferent. The optical sensors recorded the light in the corridor.

And somewhere, in the last dark room of what had once been a human being, a woman stood behind bars of titanium and screamed without a sound.
